subtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
As I was saying, there has been a considerable amount of discussion since the earlier part of the session with regard to the changed arrangements which have been made for the delivery of mail. I recognize that in a great many places the hardship which was experienced by the postmen in the earlier stages has been diminished to some extent by the gradual working out of the new system. On the other hand, I find that in some of the larger cities, and in fact in many communities across the country, there is still a good deal of objection to the change which has been made in regard to mail delivery and the carrying of the mail. It does not relate so much to the length of hours that the postmen are called upon to work, although that matter in itself is a source of objection in many cases, but rather to the fact that, particularly in the larger communities, a postman is called upon to carry a load of mail which was never contemplated in the early days when postal services were established.

Every one of us recognizes that, day by day, there is a tendency for periodical publications to increase both in size and in weight. Moreover, the people are having a larger number of periodical publications delivered to their homes by mail. I am sure that every one of the members has seen postmen carrying an enonmous load of heavy material which is largely the result of this changed arrangement. I know the answer can be given that the instructions are so worked out that this should not be the case. The fact remains, however, that whatever the instructions are, and whatever the circumstances are, I have personally had representations made to me by many postmen in different parts of this country in regard to the weight of the loads they are called upon to carry. That is particularly noticeable in the more severe weather, and of course in those areas in which the weather is more extreme.
I certainly would be the last one in the house to argue against any step that will effect economy in keeping with efficiency. I am convinced, and have said so many times, that there are a great many places where large savings can be effected in the government service. Nevertheless, in certain types of government service, efficiency must not be jeopardized by any attempt at false economy. The postmen and the post office employees generally are not only part of our whole social structure but are also a vital part of our economic structure. In addition, they are almost a part of the households of the people whom they serve. I doubt if there are any working members of the community who are brought closer, day by day, to the people whom they serve. For that very reason it is essential that this great and important service-and one which the Canadian post office has every reason to point to with pride -should not be jeopardized, nor should the excellent morale that has existed in that department over the years be impaired, by any regulations which would leave an impression in the minds of the postal employees that the value and the importance of their service were not being adequately recognized.
I do not think that the Postmaster General will question the fact that many postmen have retired from the service during these past few months. Some have been compelled to do so because of their health. No matter to what extent the earlier complaints may have been diminished in some communities, I earnestly suggest that the effect of the present arrangement on the morale and on the efficiency of the service in many other communities be carefully examined.
Having said that, from the point of view of the postmen themselves who perform an immensely valuable service for every one of
Post Office Act
us, day in and day out, in weather of all kinds, I wish to refer to the other aspect of this problem, and it is one which has not been discussed at any great length during the present session. Efficient and frequent delivery of the mail is one of the essential requirements of our modern society, and is a vitally important function within our business and economic structure. Anything which would make it less effective for the purpose of carrying on our ordinary business transactions would1 indeed be a false economy.
While I do not wish to draw comparisons unfavourably as between Canada and any other country, those who have had occasion to use the mail in London, and,'in fact, generally throughout the British isles, realize that to a great extent the mail is used over there in the place of the telegraph because frequent and prompt deliveries have made the use of the mail an efficient and effective means of immediate communication between business houses as well as between individuals, Reducing the service to one delivery a day is not only a question of economy and a question of its effect on the postman, important though that may be. It also has a marked effect on the value of that service to many business houses as well as to many functions of government at the national, the provincial or the municipal level. Over the years mail delivery here has become less frequent rather than more frequent. Yet in other countries, with the increased efficiency of the general social and economic structure, mail delivery has generally increased, both in number and in speed of deliveries.
I therefore think that this whole procedure should be re-examined and that the Postmaster General should reconsider the changes which have been made, not only from the point of view of the convenience of the postmen and of the postal organization generally, but also from the point of view of the efficiency of business throughout the whole of this country. This is particularly desirable at a time when business is to be stepped up through the addition of defence production to our ordinary civilian requirements. New burdens will be placed upon our postal service-new burdens which will have their impact upon the postmen and the postal employees generally-and also new demand's for efficient service for the more effective carrying out of the business which is done in that way. For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I strongly urge that the Postmaster General give this subject further consideration, and I can only hope that in this case the consideration may produce the same

Post Office Act
satisfactory results which ensued from our earlier arguments in regard to the cost of postal delivery of newspapers.

speechtext: I would not like the leader of the opposition to feel too certain that it was his recommendation that brought about this reduction. I have had some other people speak to me, too.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the promptness with which the Postmaster General referred to something which I had not even indicated suggests that perhaps my arguments had very considerable force with him.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
To come back to the reduction in delivery from two to one a day, there were two purposes to be accomplished by this measure. One was that of economy, and that is the one which for the most part the leader of the opposition has stressed. The other was the question of manpower. In reducing the deliveries from two to one a day we realized an economy of about 1,000 persons in the manpower field. At the outset, we felt that by making this change we could make a reduction of one out of every three men. That is to say, where three men previously served three walks and gave two deliveries a day, two men could serve the same territory by giving only one delivery a day.
We might as well face the cold facts. The service under the one-deiivery system is not as good as that which was formerly given under the two-delivery system. Some of the residential patrons, who formerly received their mail in the morning, will now receive it in the afternoon. Somebody has to be at the beginning of the route, and somebody at the end. There would be a difference of several hours in the times at which various patrons on the same route receive their mail.
The complaints, however, were not from the residential patrons; generally speaking, they accepted the reduction in good spirit. It was mainly commercial or industrial concerns, who for one reason or another were located on a residential walk, who were chiefly affected. As I said before, we hoped to have made the change by making a reduction of one man out of every three. This was found to be impracticable. It was overburdening many of our letter carriers, and causing overtime. The procedure was modified in many areas and a reduction of one in four was instituted. I might say, however, that some offices have been able to fit in the one-delivery service with a reduction of one letter carrier out of every three.
A change of this kind cannot be put into effect overnight. There are so many ramifications, involving all kinds of changes in postal arrangements. Complaints were received, but

in every case the complaint was investigated, and, where improvements could reasonably be effected, this was done immediately. The service did not involve greater travel by letter carriers, but it did involve additional loads. This was mitigated wherever possible by an adjustment of the routes, and also by having part of the load delivered to relay bundle boxes, stores and other places; we are supplying these relay bundle boxes as soon as they can be provided. In the meantime we are using stores and other places to store these bundles for the letter carriers. There was actually a certain amount of dislocation at the outset, but I do not believe this was any reason for not going ahead with the scheme.
I have received recently a report from the main letter carrier offices of Canada, and, with the exception of one or two trouble spots, the change is working out satisfactorily.
In cases where it is found by independent check that the letter carriers are working consistently more than the forty-eight hours a week, as corrected on the eleventh week to bring it to forty-four hours a week, steps will be taken to pay the letter carriers overtime for that additional period until such time as the walks can be readjusted and brought within the uniform five and a half day week.
One of the chief sore spots is Toronto. I will be perfectly frank and admit that the situation in Toronto is not as good as we could wish, but it is not entirely due to the establishment of the one delivery a day system. As a matter of fact, there was an inordinate increase in the amount of business in Toronto. The revenue for the month of April increased by $400,000 over the same month last year, or approximately twenty-eight per cent.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt, but what was the total revenue?

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Roughly $1,500,000. In addition many employees are leaving the post office to obtain employment in commercial and industrial concerns at a higher rate of pay than the post office is able to give, tied down as we are to specific rates and conditions. Improvements, however, will depend to no small extent on the department being able to obtain suitable replacements for employees who have either retired from the service on account of age, or have resigned, at the salaries and on the conditions of employment which we have to offer.
At this point I might mention that I have received a large number of letters from postal

patrons all across Canada, expressing appreciation of the adjustments made.
I wish to express a word of commendation to those employees, particularly letter carriers and city sorters, who have had to bear the brunt of this change. In most cases they have helped us loyally to put the change into effect, and I can assure the committee that it is the intention of the Post Office Department not to place any undue strain upon these employees. We shall in all cases make the adjustments as quickly as possible, but we do ask for reasonable co-operation and forbearance while the contingent adjustments are being made. I can give an assurance that we will do all we can to remedy any justifiable grievance.
To put the picture in another way, the post office cannot refuse to accept all business that is offered. When a street car gets overcrowded, the public have to wait for the next one. When the Bell Telephone have used up all the space on the circuit, patrons wishing a telephone have to wait, sometimes for months, before they can be accommodated. Stores which have sold out a particular line of goods simply say "sold out". Laundries and other organizations selling service put out signs indicating that they are unable to accommodate any more customers. The same holds true for railroads and aeroplanes. The post office, however, is expected to take on all comers, twenty-four hours a day, 365 days a year, no matter what the fluctuations in volume may be.
We have no magic formula by which we can foretell the problems of any particular period or provide necessary manpower at a time of shortage. At the present time, men are going out to the armed forces and to essential industries, and this has to be encouraged, not discouraged. All we can do is to save manpower wherever we can, and to cut out any frills. The reduction in postal deliveries was inevitable, and, unless the manpower situation eases, more restrictions may conceivably have to be considered. Everyone who has studied the basic facts will agree with the conclusions we have reached, but unfortunately most people want us to make the necessary economies, but at the expense of someone else.
Let me again make it clear, therefore, that the Post Office Department does not feel it necessary to apologize for its action in restricting service. It was brought about by conditions beyond our control. In regard to the change itself, individual mistakes and errors in carrying out the general policy will occur, and these are regretted. They are
Post Office Act
perhaps pardonable in a large and complex organization such as the postal service, extending as it does from coast to coast.
We can offer no rosy promises for immediate improvement. That will depend on conditions, but hon. members may rest assured that we shall spare no effort to give the most practical and efficient service which the resources at our disposal will permit.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the illustration offered by the Postmaster General is, I suggest, rather misleading. He says that a condition under which there is an excessive use of telephones, or street car services, or even excessive purchases in stores, can be compared with this situation. If there is a crowding of telephone lines through excessive use of those lines, or if there is a crowding of street cars to such an extent that certain people cannot get on them, or if there is sell-out of goods in a store, necessitating a would-be purchaser waiting for another occasion, the result flows from the actions of the persons seeking to obtain that service. What happened in this instance is the result of action taken by the Post Office Department itself, not by those using the service. The cure, I suggest, is exclusively within the hands of the department. In the other instances the pressure comes about because of the number of people seeking to use the service.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONSOLIDATE, CODIFY AND AMEND EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Speaking in reply to some of the observations of the Postmaster General respecting the situation in Toronto, I would say first that I was pleased to find that he is prepared to face the facts so far as that city is concerned and to admit that all is not well with the postal service in Toronto and district.
Through conversation with one of the managers of a postal station in Toronto over the week end I am inf ormed that station managers are being flooded with telephone calls and letters expressing severe criticisms of the system as it now exists, and that this condition obtains to the point where life is almost unbearable for them. At the week end immediately preceding the last one there were five routes in the constituency of South York that were not covered. Last week there was one route, in the area in which I live, on which there were no deliveries on Tuesday or Thursday. Further, a daily newspaper from Hamilton, which would be carried as second-class mail, was not delivered daily; four copies were delivered on Saturday. Naturally the citizens are complaining of a service which obliges them to accept, in one day, delivery of four issues of a newspaper which should be delivered daily.

Post Office Act
I was told by postal employees over the week end that in some of the Toronto stations neither the sorters nor the carriers have been able to keep abreast of their work. They are always behind, both in sorting and in delivering. It is obvious, therefore, that the situation in Toronto and district has not yet cleared up. It is not just a matter of having mail delivery at six or seven o'clock at night; rather it is one of having any mail delivery at all during one or two days of the week. This condition has arisen through the introduction of the one delivery a day system, which has come as a blanket order or blueprint from head office in Ottawa, without any effort to find out, through experiment in some of the larger centres, such as Toronto, just how the system would work out.
The blanket order was sent out across the country stating that the walks were to be telescoped so that one out of every three men was to be relieved, and this was done without the department having any knowledge of the disruption it would cause in the postal service. Not only has there been disruption in the system, but there has been a serious break-down in public relations. I believe in the past the Post Office Department has enjoyed as satisfactory public relations as any other department of government, but so far as my area is concerned, it has now sacrificed in large measure that satisfactory relationship.
In Toronto the change has resulted in the loss of a considerable number of permanent staff. The post office is finding it impossible to replace these experienced members with efficient help. I am informed that most of the help the department is now getting is sent from the employment offices, where the unemployed are given the choice of either taking a job with the post office or of having no unemployment insurance. The result is that not only is the Post Office Department getting inexperienced employees, but they are inefficient as well, and are thus slowing up the service.
I do not think anything can be done about retracing steps so far as the change is concerned. I am told that today it would be impossible for the Post Office Department to go back to the system of two deliveries, even if it wanted to. There is just not enough help available to reinstitute a system of two deliveries a day, even if the department so desired.	.
I was surprised to learn that the ratio of temporary to permanent employees in the Post Office Department is twenty per cent. An estimate I made in the Toronto area would indicate that the percentage of temporary to permanent employees is much higher than that. One of the complaints postal employees

are registering is that they have been kept on for years as temporary employees, without being given permanent employment, with the result that they have become disillusioned. The whole feature of permanency, as applied to the section of the civil service connected with the Post Office Department, has been destroyed, and this has had a disrupting effect upon the entire service. The department is probably doing all that can be done at the present time; but the whole trouble lies in the fact that this system of one delivery a day was instituted by headquarters at Ottawa through a blanket order applicable across the country without their first having a proper study made, and without any effort on their part to find out before the order was issued just what the effect would be in a centre like Toronto.
The minister has stated that there is competition from private enterprise in the matter of wages, and he has stated also that a shortage of manpower exists; but these things existed all through the war. During the war there was a much greater shortage of manpower than there is today, and there was the same competition from private enterprise, but there was no disruption of postal service.	We went
through the war without any disruption of that most essential service. There were good relations between the Post Office Department and the public, and there was reasonable contentment on the part of the employees with their working conditions and pay. That has been disrupted because of the steps which have been taken, and I do not think the post office is going to be able to remedy this condition for a long time to come.
I think it unfortunate that this disruption has taken place. All that can be done is for the department to continue taking the steps they are taking. I understand that surveys are being made, but it will be some time before the data collected can be tabulated and the necessary steps taken to remedy the situation. If this idea of carrying employees of the department for years on a temporary basis-this applies to other departments as well-were discontinued and employees given a permanent status after a reasonable length of time, I think the situation would be eased somewhat.
The practice of the civil service carrying over fifty per cent of its personnel for years on a temporary basis is nothing but a cheap labour racket. That is all it is. There is no reason in the world why any department should carry such a high percentage of its employees for years on a temporary basis.
In view of the situation that has developed I think the Post Office Department will have to give serious consideration to increasing

the scale of wages paid to postal employees. Never a week goes by but members of parliament receive copies of the advertisements put out by the Post Office Department for letter carriers, porters and other inside help. As the minister has said, the department is not getting enough help, and certainly is not getting the efficient type of help that it needs. This is the result partly of the disruption which has taken place, partly of the adverse advertising which the Post Office Department has received within the last two or three months, and partly of the way in which those who are employed have been subjected to working hours that are longer than necessary over a long period of time without any assurance of overtime pay.
The minister's statement last week that these employees would be paid for their overtime has had and will have a favourable effect. But I still think that before the Postmaster General can put his department on an efficient basis, consideration will have to be given to increasing the salaries paid to postal employees. Otherwise he is just not going to be able to get suitable help to enable him to give sufficient and efficient service to the public.

Mr. Chairman, I want to corroborate everything the hon. member for York South has said. Conditions almost identical to those he has mentioned exist in my district, except that they may be slightly worse. I am informed that last week there were no less than six postal walks which could not be serviced for days at a time, and that the postal authorities in Toronto had to ask members of their staff who were doing other things to fill in as postal carriers in order to have the mail delivered.
The delivery of mail transcends any dol-lars-and-cents consideration. You just cannot put it simply and solely on an economic basis. The delivery of mail is part of our economic and social life, and we cannot have it interfered with if the work of the country is to be carried on efficiently. Therefore we are faced directly with the following problem.
At the present time the Post Office Department is having great difficulty in getting personnel to handle its rapidly increasing business in the Toronto area and particularly in the suburbs as represented by the ridings of York South and York West. If men cannot be obtained to undertake this work-chiefly for economic reasons, although there are others as well-then we must be prepared either to increase the rates charged for the delivery of mail, or to have the Post Office Department operate with a deficit. There are no other ways out of the difficulty.
Post Office Act
I have found the postal authorities extremely co-operative. Every day some member of the Toronto district postal office is in York West investigating a complaint or trying to iron out some frightfully difficult situation which has arisen. In practically every case they come to me, or to the ratepayers' association or to the industry which has complained, and say that because of the regulations they cannot make the change that is asked for. If the regulations are the cause of the slowing up in postal deliveries, then I suggest that consideration should be given to altering them.
As I say, this business of the post office and the delivery of mail transcends any purely economic consideration. The carrying of heavier and heavier loads by the letter carriers is something that must be remedied. I realize that the mail is there and that it has to be carried out; but when the volume of mail becomes so great that men cannot possibly lift it and deliver it, then something must be done. With all the good will in the world on the part of the minister and the department, unless extra help is made available that mail is going to remain undelivered. It is simply a physical matter; there is not the physical strength to do the job, and unless you make it attractive enough for people to undertake this work, the situation is not going to be remedied.
I have great sympathy for the Postmaster General and his employees. I know the problems they are facing, particularly in a district such as mine, which is growing at such an extraordinary rate. I want, though, to mention once more the matter of sub-post offices. In the several cases I have brought to the attention of the minister we' thought we had all the arrangements made, but at the last moment they blew up in our faces, to use a common expression. It was impossible to get proper accommodation even after the postal authorities had toured the district. Presumably that is because the department could not offer people enough to induce them to undertake this work; and if that is because of the regulations, then the regulations should be changed so this work will be made attractive and people will undertake it. Large districts now are almost completely without mail service, or the only post office available is a considerable distance away. In my district, and I imagine this is the case around most large cities, transportation is a problem. As a result mail is now picked up perhaps once or twice a week, and collecting mail at a sub-post office is no longer a matter of a few minutes; you have to line up and wait for a half hour or more before you can get your mail. That situation is intolerable,

Post Office Act
and I think something should be done, either through the civil service commission or the department itself, so that this work, which is just as essential as any other work in Canada, may be carried on efficiently.
Finally I would ask the Postmaster General if he can give me the wage scale in three principal classifications of employees, mail porters, postal delivery men and some other classification, in 1939 and today. Then I have this suggestion to make: that if we cannot clear up the situation through the present machinery, a committee of this house be set up next session so that the whole question of the Post Office Department may be gone into. Whether it means we shall have to pay more for the service, or that the post office will have to operate at a deficit, the facts should be presented to this parliament so that the people of Canada will know what they are facing. They should know whether the present intolerable conditions have come about because of the regulations, or because of inflationary pressure or for what other reason, and whether they will have to accept either an increase in the rates or be prepared to have the post office operate at a loss. These are technical problems which I believe should be considered next session by a committee of this house.

When the Postmaster General was making some remarks a little while ago he referred to men going into the armed forces. He did not say whether or not there was objection to this, but there is a question I want to ask in that connection. This morning I received a letter from a permanent civil servant, a railway mail clerk operating from Charlottetown to Sackville. On May 29 he enlisted in the active army for three years, with the understanding that he would go with the 27th infantry brigade. This man had fourteen years of service with the post office and three and one-half years in the last war, and here is his complaint. The operations branch of the postal department of Ottawa wrote the inspector at Charlottetown stating that the civil service commission had not yet issued orders that a civil servant may enlist in the armed forces; the civil service commission did not issue leave of absence covering the men who enlisted in the 25th until lately, and those who have enlisted in the 27th have not been granted this leave of absence by the postal department. His question is: Will he, by going overseas, have lost his job, and will he also lose out on his retiring allowance?
I do not know anything about this man except that he appears to be a genuine civil servant, and I should like to know whether the department issues these letters to men

who sign up. It would certainly break down their morale if that is the practice. I believe this man and others in the same position should be given some satisfaction as soon as possible.
The answer to the question is contained in what the hon. member just read. The civil service commission has not yet given a clear directive as to what must be done.
Is the Post Office Department governed by the civil service commission in regard to men joining the armed forces?

Not only that, but also in respect to appointments.
With regard to the question I was asked a minute ago by the hon. member for York West, a comparison of salaries, for the sake of simplification I shall give the maximum salaries. In 1939 for carriers the remuneration was $1,500; in 1950, $2,628; porters, $1,500 and $2,496; clerks, $1,740 and $2,904.

Will the Postmaster General
tell me whether the $2,628 for mail carriers is the salary in the largest office?
Yes, of course.

Why is there a differential
in the salary scale between a town like Port Alberni and the city of Vancouver?
It is a question of revenue.

One of the great difficulties
we have had in Port Alberni is the obtaining of mail carriers. In the district we have one of the highest wage rates in Canada. The saw mills pay $1.40 per hour, so we have difficulty in obtaining letter carriers. Why should the revenue of the office be the standard for setting the remuneration of a man who is doing comparable work to that which is performed in a larger office? Is that a sound basis?

That is the only standard
we have to go by. If we increase the salaries in one part of the country, we have to be prepared to do the same thing throughout the rest of the country. If we increase the salary scale for Port Alberni, we would have to be prepared to do the same thing for a similar office situated in the east.

I should like to ask one
more question with reference to the answer I got to the last one. I do not think it is satisfactory. I want to send a telegram to this man; have I got to go back to the civil service commission and consult them about this employee? I believe the postal department should have some control in this matter; instead of a member taking it up,

the department should take it up. Surely this veteran is entitled to a straight answer so that he can try to get out of the army and get back to his employment, or so that he will know what is going to happen to him.

The answer to the first question is yes. The answer to the second question is that the hon. member can be assured that as soon as we get the necessary directive there will be no delay in the post office giving him his letter.

There will be no delay in
receiving that from the commission; are we assured of that?
That will be a directive from the civil service commission, and I cannot answer that.

I am pleased to hear the
Postmaster General say that the situation is continuously being reviewed to correct mistakes. From what has happened, it is obvious that his department took hasty action without sufficient thought. I think it was unfortunate action, because it was taken in connection with one of the lower paid groups of employees. As the Postmaster General knows, it has caused a good many men to leave the service of the Post Office Department.
I had a few words to say on this matter on an occasion when we had the opportunity to raise grievances. But since that time I have had a number of letters from trade union organizations in the cities of Trail and Nelson, bringing to my attention the particularly difficult circumstances under which mail carriers work in that area. These two cities, Mr. Chairman, are situated on the sides of mountains. The mail carriers have to carry mail on routes which in many cases have grades of up to thirty per cent. In addition to that, in climbing from one street to another there are steps that are on a forty-five degree angle, and of such a height that they would reach from the base of the parliament buildings to the top of the tower. If the deputy postmaster general had to carry one of these sacks of mail up these steps we would get the matter rectified very quickly.
It is easy to make plans for level communities like Ottawa, but in that area we have particularly difficult conditions. I ask that the whole question be reconsidered so far as that locality is concerned. I realize the necessity for saving where possible, but the problem is so serious in my district that not only have labour organizations been writing to me, but elderly ladies, who have 80709-248
Post Office Act
seen the postmen going along the streets, write to say that the Post Office Department is making poorly paid pack horses out of our letter carriers. I believe this shows that the change of route was made without sufficient consideration. I ask that the matter be reviewed in that district, because of the exceptional conditions under which these mail carriers work.
I should like to ask the Postmaster General by whose recommendation these changes are made in any given locality. At what level is that official? Who is responsible for the final decision? I am quite sure that no one who was directly informed as to the circumstances that exist in the cities of Trail and Nelson would have made the changes in the first instance. I believe there has been some improvement, but there is a necessity for more improvement if these men are to be treated fairly.
I should like to say a word in support of the remarks made by the member for Comox-Alberni, who at times does make some contribution to the debate in this house. In his remarks the Postmaster General indicated that a number of the employees were leaving his department because they could get higher rates of pay in industry. That is happening in the district I have the honour to represent, because there is a relatively high wage scale in that area. Lumbering, mining and smelting pay relatively high wages in Canada compared to those received by the letter carriers. This means that only the older men, who cannot obtain employment in the woods, mines or smelters, are going to apply for these positions. Older men who do this type of work will find it a greater burden than some of the younger men who have resigned because they were able to take heavier jobs. I believe that is going to increase the difficulties of the department; and in this connection I did want t,o bring to the attention of the Postmaster General the unusual and serious conditions in the cities in my constituency.

While I sympathize with these people in Toronto and other places who are only getting their mail once a day instead of twice, I want to say a word for some people in other parts of this dominion who were getting their mail twice a week and now are not getting it at all. In certain rural areas in my constituency, I believe four or five of these rural routes that were in operation five or six years ago are now closed. Only one route is operating today.
In those cases where rural routes are established, the courier travels from thirty to thirty-five miles, seventeen miles out and seventeen miles back. Quite often there was a rural post office serving the community

Post Office Act
before the routes were established, and now that these routes have been discontinued the rural post offices have not been re-established. This leaves many people from fifteen to twenty miles from the closest post office.
The reason given for closing most of these routes is that people will not bid on the contracts for the delivery of mail. The contracts are usually let at from $700 to $750 for a year. That, is not much of an income, and it is very seldom that these people can take on much other work. They have to attend to these routes two days a week, and they have to maintain equipment, either a car or a truck for the delivery of the mail. They have to deliver it in all kinds of weather conditions, winter and summer. The result has been that many of these rural routes are closed. Will the minister give us the number of routes in Saskatchewan that have been closed during the last five years, and the number of new routes that have been established?
Speaking earlier in the debate, one of the members said that the delivery of mail should transcend purely economic considerations. I believe that, and I believe that the people in rural areas, who live there because they must do so in order to produce the food for the rest of this dominion, are entitled to better mail delivery service than they are getting at the present time. I bring the matter to the minister's attention because I think a mistake has been made in the closing of the number of rural routes that have been closed in western Canada during the last few years.
On that point, I may say to the hon. member for Melfort that not one single rural route in Canada pays its own way.
I realize that.

And as to the post offices, the great majority of them do not pay their way. We are therefore giving more service than is justified by the revenue we are receiving.
On the question of the closing of post offices, it has been discovered that, with the increase of the rural routes, so few people were served by post offices in small towns-four, five or six-we thought it was good economy to serve everybody by the rural route rather than have the post offices remain open.
If, as the hon. member suggests, there are some of these rural routes that have been abandoned, if he will kindly send me the names of them I will see that the post offices are reopened.
I thank the minister for that. But again I want to point out that you cannot put the matter on a purely economic basis.
We do not. That is exactly what I said.

Nor can you use the argument that you do not realize adequate revenue. The revenue for those routes may come from the city of Winnipeg, because it is from there that a great deal of the mail is sent which is received over these routes. You have no way of determining their value. Therefore I do not think it is fair to put the matter on an economic basis. The basis on which we should operate the post offices is the basis of service to the most people in the Dominion of Canada.
That is exactly what we do.
You are not doing it altogether. I should like to see you do it just a little bit more than is being done now, having regard to rural mail delivery.

For the last fifteen or twenty minutes, Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting to say what the hon. member for Melfort has just said. In that case it was Wright; now it is Fair and Wright. I hope the Postmaster General and his deputy will take notice of what the hon. member for Melfort has just said.
And what is fair.

And what is supported by Fair. During the early part of this sitting we listened to discussion of the difficulties in the cities. It is not my intention for one moment to oppose mail delivery in the cities once or twice a day. I am fully aware that this service is necessary; and I was sorry when the Postmaster General and his colleagues found it necessary to eliminate one of the services in many of the cities that had been receiving twice-a-day service. But I think the minister will agree that if it were not for the rural population in Canada there would not be any need for either towns or cities all across this country. They are there for the service of the rural communities. The sooner we recognize that fact, the sooner perhaps will better service be given to the rural communities in postal and other matters.
There is a problem, I believe, all across Canada with regard to rural routes being shut down at least temporarily. In my own case I have been dealing for some little time with the other officials of the department. I have not yet brought the matter to the attention of the Postmaster General or his deputy, and I am not doing so now. But apparently the practice has been that where contracts expire and tenders are called for again, if in the opinion of the officials administering the service, a tender is too high, they wait for a

while and again, in some cases after pressure is brought to bear upon them, call for new tenders. If those tenders still are too high, they let the matter drift, with the idea perhaps that somebody will be foolish enough to put in a tender on which he will lose money and still continue the service. That is one of the things to which I take serious objection. Where a tender is too high, I feel that at least the service should be continued until somebody is found who will put in a satisfactory tender.
In one case in which I am particularly interested I know that the tender put in is not too high, but because it is higher than it was four years ago the people on that particular route are obliged to go without service. That situation is now running into the third month. Yet when those people are attempting at the present time to take off last year's crop and to sow another crop for harvesting this year, they are compelled to go quite a number of miles for their mail. They are left without service simply because we must economize in the Post Office Department.
I understand that that complaint is general from the Atlantic to the Pacific in, connection with rural mail routes. A little later on I will perhaps take this particular case up with the deputy minister, and later, if necessary, with the minister. I am not mentioning any names at the present time. But again I want to support the complaint that has been made by the hon. member for Melfort. The Postmaster General will hear from me a little later on unless service is restored in the near future.

As the minister knows, the main post office in Newfoundland is the general post office in St. John's. The next important post office is known as the east end branch at St. John's. It is in connection with the operation of the east end branch of the general post office in St. John's that I want to speak for a few moments.
I have had a letter from a prominent newspaper man in St. John's; and in order that there may be no misunderstanding about the matter, may I say that it is a newspaper that supports the government. It is in connection with what he writes that I wish to speak; I want to draw the contents of his letter to the minister's attention. In his letter he states:
Since we joined Canada the postal service has deteriorated. For example, the east end branch has been catering to a growing clientele . . . We are within eighty yards of that post office but have had to transfer our business to the general, a mile away. Why? Several reasons. One, mail dropped into the east end, even if for boxholders there, is sent to the general for franking and then returned
80709-248|
Post Office Act
to the east end. Think of the delay here; at least a day. The east end does not cash money orders, although it will sell them; and neither will it give out parcels. Air mails are sometimes not delivered until the next day if arriving at the general late in the afternoon. The east end is not open at night as it used to be ... it is impossible to pick up mail after regular business hours. The other night, after I heard Mr. St. Laurent's message to the Commons, I wrote an article for-
A Canadian company, a mainland newspaper.
-and posted it at the general at 10.30 p.m. The caretaker said, the air mail had been picked up for the next plane which was not going out until 1.30 or 2 a.m., and my letter would have to wait for the next plane, not before noon. Why the long delay between closing-off time and the departure of the planes? The airport is no more than twenty minutes slow driving, from the city, and midnight would be ample time to close off reception of mail. It must be emphasized, of course, that the present poor mail service is not due to the staff. They are the same as pre-confederation when we had a better distribution and the east end was open day and night, Sundays and holidays. The new order came in shortly after union and is the work of Ottawa. The carrier system has also been cut down to one delivery a day.
I will not go any further into the matter, except to emphasize once again that this branch serves not only a large part of the business community of St. John's, but also a considerable number of the outlying settlements. I feel that the minister is fully aware of that fact. I should like him to take the matter into consideration. I do not know whether he can give me an answer now.

I will certainly take the matter into consideration. As to what is right and fair, the number of rural routes that have been increased in the last four years is 237. The number of persons served is 65,000 more than it was in 1946.
May I ask the minister how many routes have been discontinued temporarily all across the country?
I have not that figure; I will endeavour to get it.

I was going to ask the same question. I might add that I had a note here to make some remarks along the same lines as those made by the hon. member for Melfort and the hon. member for Battle River, but we in the maritimes have always had to take second place to the west. The greatest curse we have is our modesty.
It has seemed to me for some time that there was a peculiar situation in this country when in the towns and cities the people could get delivery of mail twice a day, and in the country districts many of them, as the hon. member for Melfort has said, get delivery of mail twice a week. That was the complaint that I wished to make.

Post Office Act
Frankly, I wish to congratulate the Postmaster General on having changed the system to only one delivery of mail a day in the cities. In the past there has been very great discrimination all over this country so far as delivery of mail is concerned. There is no reason in the world why people living in a city or a large town should receive their mail both in the morning and in the afternoon, while the people living in the country districts receive it perhaps two or three times a week.
It is a difficult matter to keep people in the country and on the farms. The receiving of mail, the receiving of the daily papers, as pointed out by the leader of the opposition the other day, is an encouragement to people to remain in the country districts. I repeat that I heartily support the statements made by the hon. member for Battle River and the hon. member for Melfort.
I have a question with regard to the appointment of postmasters. I think some of them are called revenue postmasters in the smaller towns. Once a postmaster is appointed, has he the authority to appoint his assistants and helpers? Are they appointed by the civil service commission?

The other day we went fully into the system of appointment of postmasters. In some instances the assistants in the large post offices in the revenue division are appointed directly by the civil service commission. In smaller revenue post offices, recommendations are made by the postmasters, which are sent to us, and we either accept them or reject them, as the case may be. In all cases they are paid by the department.
My understanding was that in some instances a postmaster was allowed a certain amount for the expenses of his post office, and out of that his salary came, and he also employed his help.
That has been changed in recent years.

Anyway, I have had complaints from different sections that people appointed, sometimes not by the civil service commission but through the postmaster or in some other way, were not altogether satisfactory and efficient. The public have made that complaint. What supervision or check-up has the minister's department over these employees who have been appointed in this manner?
While I am on my feet I wish to ask the minister a question with reference to the delivery of mail to summer residents. The minister knows that in the summer a great many people go out from the towns and cities

to summer houses, and there has to be a change in the delivery of mails. I know of some instances. I refer in particular to Kennebecasis island near Saint John, where in the wintertime there are only one or two families, but in the summer there are forty-five or more summer residents. The post office was closed. What provision does the minister's department make in cases of that kind?

In some places where there are a sufficient number of vacationers we do establish summer post offices.
As to the other question that the hon. member asked, our inspectors keep an official check on all these assistants as they go along.

What basis is used in setting the remuneration of a postmaster in a small country point? I ask that question because several cases have been drawn to my attention in which the rates appear to be scandalously low. A year ago I drew the attention of the department to one small hamlet, namely, Lanfine, where they were advertising that they would have to close the post office unless they received an application for the job of postmaster. The reason they had such a great deal of difficulty in getting an application for that job was that they were paying actually less than $1 a day. Naturally it is not easy to get a man in there at that rate.
Then I have another point. In a larger village they are paying $83 a month, but out of that the postmaster has to pay rent for the building and the cost of fuel and light. It is not a living wage. I know that preference is given to veterans, and where a veteran is getting a fairly high pension he may be able to do this job and make a living. Surely we should be able to pay a rate which would make it possible for a postmaster to make a living out of the job, instead of using pensioners in the form of cheap labour.
I realize that the revenue from some of these points may be very small, but on the other hand, while these hamlets may be small they do provide a service for a large area, and it seems to me that there should be some minimum below which the remuneration should not be allowed to fall. What is the basis?

The question is threefold, as I see it. First of all, these small offices are paid in relation to revenue. Second, the revenue in each of these small offices to which my hon. friend refers is invariably below the salary that we pay to the postmasters. Third, the hon. member has referred to the fact that these postmasters have to pay for light, heat, and so forth. Over and

above the salary we do pay a rental allowance to cover these costs. Fourth, and most important, the job of these postmasters is not considered to be a full-time job. They are given a certain amount, not to cover the salaries on the basis of a full-time job- it is not an amount sufficient for them to live on-but something extra that we pay them to carry on part-time jobs. I think that is the answer.

This may not be the opportune time to ask for anything, after hearing the complaints of various members, but I am really concerned about my constituency, because it is one which is growing by leaps and bounds, and has for the last few years. Postal services have not grown along with it. I should like to draw the minister's attention to the municipality of Charleswood, where they have no mail service. The people who are living in Charleswood have been used to mail service. They were the original settlers in Charleswood. Now we have gradually moved the people from Winnipeg into the suburbs, and they do not have that service. The minister's department was good enough to give me all the necessary papers in connection with getting the service, but things always seemed to crop up-perhaps they did not have a cement sidewalk, or something like that. I am wondering if it would be possible to have a rural mail service in that area. Perhaps it would not be suitable, but surely something can be done. I am asking the minister now if he would be good enough to encourage the general post office in Winnipeg to continue the survey of the district.
i have talked both to the minister and to his deputy about jumping-off places; but the jumping-off place three or four years ago is certainly not the jumping-off place today. While the department is studying ways of economizing it wants to maintain the old jumping-off place. I would ask the minister in all sincerity if he would have a survey of West Kildonan and St. James, and see if something cannot be done by way of supplying a mail service to Charleswood.
I shall certainly do that.

Some discussion has taken place about remuneration for different sizes of towns. I can understand that a postmaster's remuneration should be on that basis, because, after all, a post office with a revenue of $20,000 does not entail as much administrative work as one with a revenue of $40,000. On the other hand, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Kootenay West, it is possible that in the smaller towns it would be even more difficult for the letter carriers. In those
Post Office Act
smaller towns sidewalks might not be in as good condition, and transportation facilities would not be as satisfactory. I do not think it is fair to assume that because the revenue of an office is down, the letter carriers do not do as much work as is done by the carriers in the cities. I know that a worker in a small saw mill will have to work harder than a worker in a large saw mill. The man in a large and efficient saw mill would have to do less work. I ask the minister if he would discuss this matter with a view to working out a proper basis for letter carriers.
It is not a question of discussing it with my officials, because they are convinced in the matter. It is a question of discussing it with the civil service commission and having its approval.
You will consider doing that?
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, I wish all the people across Canada who voted Tory at the last election could be here to listen to the discussion in the committee this morning. They must be nodding their heads, in those forty-two constituencies which elected Tory candidates, and saying, "I told you so; I told you so." Certainly they must, when they realize the condition of the Post Office Department, and when it is proven, by fact and statement from one end of the country to the other, that it is inefficient, and that inefficiency now prevails. It must be a great laugh for those people who voted for the Tory party; there is no doubt about it.
We find a man volunteering to fight for his country, a man who writes, and properly so, to his member of parliament-and if those gentlemen behind the curtains will be a little quieter, I will proceed. We find a man who has joined the armed forces of this country writing a letter in which he tries to find out whether he is going to be penalized for daring to volunteer. And, according to the statement of the Postmaster General, all this is in the hands of the civil service commission. Instead of the Postmaster General being able to speak for the government and being in a position to say that a man who occupied a position in Canada, and who volunteered and is accepted in His Majesty's forces, will be able to return to the same position, and with the same seniority as he held before, it is referred to the civil service commission. We are told in the House of Commons today that this is left to the good graces of the civil service commission.
That is not so in all cases. We see that the commission, that great body of geniuses, is not consulted about appointments to smaller post offices. All that is passed on for political

Post Office Act
plums and recommendations. But our soldiers do not receive the benefit of political plums. They must wait for the civil service commission to see whether they are to be properly remunerated if they dare to volunteer for service in the armed forces.
Well, any of those people in the forty-two constituencies that elected Tory representatives must be laughing at the people in all the other constituencies across this country. And I say this, that at the next election the people of Canada will remember. They will remember the laughter of the forty-two constituencies who voted for Tory candidates. They will remember where the government of Canada stood when it came to treatment of soldiers serving overseas. This is only the beginning of the proof of the fact that this government, in all its departments, is deteriorating at a speed the people will soon recognize.
The postal department is a monopoly, and all the people of Canada must rely upon it for the delivery of mail. What are we getting? We have the undoubted and proven fact that there is not any department in any kind of activity that is as lax and inefficient as is the Post Office Department. I do not blame the Postmaster General. He is a man who is trying to do his job. He is a man with ability, and he is doing a good job in his department-and one must recognize that fact when he considers the lack of foresight and planning shown by the government.
This lack first became clear in connection with immigration. The representatives of [DOT]those forty-two constituencies have stated repeatedly on the floor of the House of Commons that we should keep pace with the growing demands of our country and of Canadians. We have pointed out that we need an increased population, and that we should increase our immigration to meet the required expansion. But we have heard members of the Liberal party state openly in the house that, while we should increase our population, they want to have it done in the natural way, and not . through the importation of immigrants from foreign lands. We now see the fallacy of that teaching. We find ourselves short of labour in all branches of government, including the Post Office Department.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. This is a debate in connection with the Canada Post Office Act.

All right, Mr. Chairman; I have included the post office. I could go on for an hour repeating complaints, justifiable complaints, and listening to explanations from the Postmaster General as to why we 
have this mess under which people receive their daily papers only once in four days. They are not having the required two-a-day delivery in cities, so that they could cope with their general business, and so that they could continue to compete in international trade. This simply cannot be done in the larger cities, where the mail is dumped at offices and delivered to factories only once a day. It is impossible during one period of the morning to attend to the mail for the entire twenty-four hours. It must be 'broken up, not only for the convenience of delivery, but so that it may be handled intelligently by those who receive it.
In the great city of Toronto people are receiving their mail two or three days late. This is not a condition that has grown up in the last two or three years. It is one that has finally developed after ten years of Liberal administration, and the unemployment brought about by the Liberal government in 1939. Because of the war brought on by Hitler there was some prosperity, but now we return to this condition brought about by the mismanagement of the Liberal party.

Section 5(b) refers to the
authority of the minister in the matter of making appointments. I should like to ask the minister if it is true that postmasters of accounting offices are appointed through the civil service commission.

It is not a question whether
it is an accounting office; it is a question of revenue. All appointments to offices having an annual revenue of $3,000 and over are made through the civil service commission.
The minister has indicated that the compensation paid to postmasters in certain offices is determined by the revenue of the office; is that correct?
That is correct.

Could we have the formula
that is used? For example, I notice that the revenue of different post offices varies considerably. The post office in my own home town had a revenue of $18,000 last year, whereas another post office in my constituency had a revenue of $26,000. What formula is used in determining the salary to be paid to the postmaster? I am not referring to those two cases specifically, but to post offices generally.
By what method are members of the staffs appointed, and how is their remuneration determined?
The same method.
What about hours of labour and compensation for overtime?

Where overtime can be
checked, it is paid at the regular rate, but in the case of certain positions, such as letter
carriers, where no check can be made of the time sipent, usually we do not pay overtime. As I indicated last week, following the inauguration of the one mail service per day we are having official checkers go over the route. When it is found that any one route necessitates regular overtime, overtime will be paid.

I was referring to employees in the post office itself rather than to the mail

Post Office Act
carriers. What rate is used to compute the overtime paid in various offices, accounting and non-accounting?
It is computed on the basis of a forty-four hour week.
Is the compensation paid for overtime the regular rate?
Yes.
Is it simply a matter of the postmaster in a local post office reporting to the district office that such and such an employee has worked overtime; is it as simple as that?
Just about as simple as that.
I want to get this perfectly clear. They are just paid the regular rate for overtime?
Exactly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Not time and a half?
No.
I assume the rate of compensation would be arrived at by dividing the weekly rate by forty-four hours, and that would be paid for overtime?
That is correct.

Section 5 (1) (a) provides for the establishment and closing of post offices. I think the Postmaster General will agree that the closing of a small post office may be a serious matter. Two post offices were closed in my constituency, and if the department had come to me in the first place and asked my opinion they would not have closed them and then have had to reopen them. I believe the department's source of information is not sufficiently reliable to warrant the closing of a post office without first obtaining the viewpoint of those who represent the people.
Paragraph (c) (iv) provides for the payment of indemnities. I should like to know how the indemnity is fixed. Paragraph (e) provides for the removal of postal employees. The Postmaster General seems to have power to dismiss employees, and I should like to know whether such employees have any court of appeal to which they can go. I know of cases in other departments where men have been let out without a proper inquiry being made, with the result that they have lost all the money they had paid in. Men have been dismissed for some political whim, with the results I have mentioned.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
TMr. Shaw.]
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

When the committee took recess at one o'clock I was asking one or two questions. Section 5(l)(h) provides that the Postmaster General may-
-authorize agents to sell to the public postage stamps and stamped forms and envelopes and allow to such agents a commission not exceeding two per cent of the amount of their sales.
.Last year in this connection I brought to the attention of the minister the breaking of the contract with the stamp vendor in Charlottetown. That man has given some fifty-one years of service in selling stamps to the people of Charlottetown and vicinity. Actually it is more than fifty-one years; on the basis of an eight-hour day he has given over seventy-five years of service, and now the department is trying to get rid of him. My objection is to the way they are breaking their contract with him so that he will not be able to make a living and will have to resign.
Over fifty years ago this man signed a contract with the Postmaster General for this concession. That contract is still in force, and I do not think it can be broken even under this bill, in which so much authority is granted the minister. How are they breaking it? I have no objection to meter machines, but at the same time the operation of these machines has reduced this man's earning capacity, since the department are not paying him on the postage sold by these machines, as they should according to the contract. They may say he is not selling stamps, but the postage issued by a meter is recognized by the department, and he should be paid his commission on that postage.
Here is the way it affects him. He has never made very high wages, and I went over the details with him so I could make a comparison over the last five years. As I said before, this man had an agreement with the Postmaster General calling for payment of a commission of two per cent on all stamps sold. Today there are probably thirty-five meter machines in the large business houses of Charlottetown. In 1945 Mr. Brown sold $135,630 worth of stamps, on which he received his two per cent commission. Then the meter machines were put in, and their number has gradually increased. This has reduced his sale of stamps to a little over $100,000. There is a difference of some $25,000 or more on which he has lost tne commission, and in that way his salary has been reduced from an average of about $2,600 to about $2,000. In other words the department have reduced this man's earning power and benefited themselves by some $600 a year.

II they want to get rid of this man, why not give him a small pension for the rest of his days? Even at best they will not be long, and already the department owes him at least $2,500 which has been taken from him by breaking the contract. Suppose this man had not been efficient; suppose he had in some way broken the contract; how long would he have lasted with the department? I want the minister and those who are coaching him to understand this.
This is a repetition of last year, so I know it.

I want you to see the injustice you are doing to a good citizen of this country. This man puts in twelve hours a day, though I believe he has been given an extra half hour off recently. He has no dinner hour, no rest periods of any kind. If he goes out he must pay an assistant. If he wants one or two holidays a year he has to pay an assistant. He has given excellent service. A year ago he was honoured by the city on having completed fifty years of service without a demerit of any kind. I doubt if a score of people in the department have a record as good. Last year, according to the record, I was promised that some consideration would be given him. But there was a qualifying phrase-that he was not an employee of the department. According to these new regulations, however, I believe he is now an employee, so that'excuse is washed out and consideration surely can be given to Aubrey F. Brown, the stamp vendor in the post office at Charlottetown. Suppose you do force him out and sell the stamps at the postal wicket; that will not be an economy measure, because it will cost the department twice as much. These men all work an eight-hour day, while stamps must be sold during twelve hours of the day. I want the Postmaster General to give me some statement to indicate that justice and fair play will be meted out to one of the best officials in the department-in Charlottetown, Ottawa or anywhere else. I hope the minister has thought of it in time to give some consideration to this matter.

The member for Queens
referred to a matter before the recess at one o'clock which I think calls for an answer. He suggested that people were dismissed from the Post Office Department for political reasons-or political whims, I think he said- without any sort of inquiry. That might have been true years ago, but it is not true any longer. The circumstances surrounding the dismissal of any person for these considerations are inquired into by a board appointed by the Department of Justice. It makes a
Post Office Act
report one way or the other. The Postmaster General has no say in it, but has to follow the report of this board of inquiry.
Now, as to the other question asked by the member for Queens, it concerns the same matter that he brought up last year. This man is a contractor for the department and not an employee. The present act does not make him an employee. The hon. member has to decide whether or not it is a contract, because in part of his argument he said the man was receiving some sort of salary. He is receiving compensation on a contract. When we are acting with a contractor, we cannot give him any sort of pension.

That is quite right, Mr. Chairman. I did not say he was receiving a salary. He is on a commission basis. What I ask is that the department fulfil the contract, and not rob him of $500 or $600 a year which it is giving to someone who is making the meter machines. If he is not an employee you cannot deal otherwise with him, but are you not duty bound to live up to your agreement? It was entered into about fifty-one years ago. I should like to know whether or not you will give him the two per cent commission on all stamps sold, according to the terms of the contract.

I shall have to review the file. I have not looked at it since last year. I will see what I can do.
This morning the hon. member for Queens referred to a letter concerning a certain man, and I told him we were awaiting some directive from the civil service commission giving authority to permit this man to join the forces, and indicating whether he could come back to the service with the same priorities and privileges as he had. While the hon. member was on his feet, the department received the necessary directives, and we shall put them into operation immediately.
I thank you for that. There are several others in the same category, and I shall inform them all.
How many vending contractors do you have? Why should the Post Office Department not own and operate these vending machines?

That is the aim, and is one of the reasons why the number of these vending licences is going down all the time. I am sorry that" I have not the exact number of licensees, but our aim is to restrict them as much as possible, so as to have all the operations under the post office itself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to pursue for a few minutes a matter that I
3912

Post Office Act
referred to on May 29. Before I do so I should like, as a city member, to support the plea that was made this morning by my deskmate, the hon. member for Melfort, and other members from rural ridings, for the best possible postal service in rural areas. I, for one, do not believe it is fair to judge a rural post office by the amount of revenue it derives from the sale of stamps. After all, it seems to me you have to take into consideration, particularly in western Canada, the amount of revenue that is taken in at Winnipeg, for example from the T. Eaton Company and other people, from the large volume of parcels and mail that is circulated in rural areas. If the mail order houses or some of the newspapers had to pay the actual cost of delivering their parcels or their periodicals to rural areas, the revenue from these sources at city centres would amount to a great deal. I want to support the position taken this morning by a number of members from rural areas. It does seem to me that this is one service we have to look at on an over-all basis. It is not a case of being able to ascertain whether or not each little district pays, but we are dealing with a service to the people of Canada. I believe it should be so regarded.
The matter I particularly wanted to pursue for a few minutes is one that I drew to the attention of the Postmaster General on the second reading of this bill. My remarks will be found commencing at page 3532 of Hansard for May 29. I refer to the case of mail couriers in the city of Winnipeg who work for contractors whose contracts are let under the provisions of the section with which we are now dealing, section 5, subsection 1, paragraph (o).
As I indicated on other occasions when I dealt with these mail couriers, the men who drive about in Winnipeg in what appear to be post office vehicles, picking up the mail from street letter boxes, are not employees of the post office at all, nor are the vehicles owned by the Post Office Department. These men are employees of the local contractor who contracted with the Post Office Department. Accordingly, the Post Office Department does not directly set the wages * or working conditions of those employees. The Post Office Department has some indirect influence on the wages and working conditions of these employees, because the contractors are able to pay such wages and provide such conditions as they feel they can provide out of the amount of the contract. .
To get down to the proverbial brass tacks, I should like to indicate to the committee some of the conditions under which these

men work. May I point out that their numbers, particularly in Winnipeg, are few. In fact, the latest information I have is that there are about thirty-five classed as mail couriers, the men who drive these vehicles about, picking up mail from letter boxes and performing certain related services. There will be a similar number of them in other cities of a similar size, and more of them in the larger cities. In Winnipeg, these men work for a rate of 83 cents per hour. I have before me information, for some eight or ten other employers in the city of Winnipeg, as to the rates of wages paid to people doing comparable work. For example, I have the rates for civic employees driving trucks. I have the rates for the Manitoba Cartage Company, Canadian Pacific Express Company, the Coca Cola Company, Thomas Jackson Fuel Company, McCurdy Fuel and Building Supplies, Winnipeg packing plants and so on. All of these other firms are paying wages higher than 83 cents an hour, which is the rate paid to these Winnipeg postal couriers. One of these firms, it is true, has a starting rate that is less than 83 cents an hour but after six months that firm's rate is 86 cents an hour; and that is the lowest of all the rates. But the rate paid by these post office contractors-not paid directly by the government but by the contractors that get a contract from the Post Office Department-is 83 cents an hour. There are no changes in that rate for additional service. That is the rate at which they start and that is the rate at which they are paid, no matter how many years they have been doing this work.
These men get no overtime pay. It is not a case of their getting time and a half or double time. They do not even get straight time for overtime pay. They do not get pay for legal holidays. If they get a legal holiday off, there is no pay for it. If they are required to work on a legal or statutory holiday, they get only straight time. They have no sick leave. They have no pension plan, although there is some group insurance. They get no pay for the period of time between trips. Let me put it this way. In order to draw their eight hours' pay, these men are required to be actually driving eight hours during the course of the day. But they are not permitted to work that eight hours simply by going in at eight o'clock in the morning and quitting at five o'clock in the afternoon. They actually have to be on trips to an aggregate of eight hours. The time in between trips that they may have to sit around in the post office waiting for the next trip to be made is not paid for. These men tell me that many of them have to put in up to twelve hours on the job in order to get in eight

hours for which they get paid, and that at the rate of 83 cents an hour. They get one week's holidays with pay; and that same one week with pay is all they get, no matter how many years they may have been in the employ of the contractor for whom they work.
Again I may say that if one goes over the chart that I have here showing the rates of pay and the working conditions for comparable work in the city of Winnipeg of these other employees, on the score of holidays with pay and on every other score those working for the other firms do much better than do these men. They are doing an important work, an important service to the people of Canada. We depend heavily on the work that all our postal employees do. The handling of the mail is an important task, and what could be more important than picking it up from the street letter boxes and seeing to it that it gets to the central post office and so on? Yet the general public tends to think of them as post office employees and tends to assume that they get whatever conditions of pay and employment go with service in the Post Office Department.
When these employees complain about their rates of pay or their working conditions -for example if they bring the matter to the attention of a member of parliament and the member of parliament brings it to the attention of the Post Office Department-the immediate reply is:	These are not our
employees; they are the employees of certain contractors in the city of Winnipeg and it is to those contractors that the men must appeal for any improvements that they desire. On occasion the contractors have been impressed with the plight of their employees and have asked the Post Office Department for an upward adjustment in the contract so that they could pay better wages. The request of the contractor is not always granted, and the contractor does not always make the request. There are times when he just gives to the employees his own answer that nothing can be done about it.
