To the credit of the Post Office Department I want to say that I know of one or two cases in which they have increased the amount of the contract with the specific understanding that it would be used to improve the wages of the employees of the contractors. But the position of these employees, as to conditions of employment and wages, is forever lagging behind that of men doing comparable work.
One answer to this problem of an immediate nature might be for the department to agree to increase the amount of the contract in cities like Winnipeg or any other cities where a similar situation obtains. But that does not solve the problem on any permanent 80709-249J
Post Office Act
basis. It seems to me that the only solution to this problem is for the Post Office Department itself to take over this work of collecting the mail from the street letter boxes and the various delivery services that have to be made in bulk, by trucks and vehicles of one sort and another. Taking that work over would involve making these mail couriers employees of the Post Office Department. I feel that should be done so that these men can get proper wages for the work they are doing, and so that they can get sick leave, statutory holidays with pay, pension privileges, and the other rights and benefits that go with the doing of government work. After all, that is what -they are doing. They are working for the government or for the people of this country. I think they should have that status rather than the status of being employees of private contractors.
I have taken this matter up with the Postmaster General a number of times by letter, as is obvious from the thickness of the file I am turning over as I speak. On one or two occasions the Postmaster General has indicated to me by letter that consideration was being given to the request that this work be taken over by the Post Office Department, and that these men be made employees of the Post Office Department. I should be glad to hear from him now what the result of that consideration is. I hope that it is favourable. I hope that action may be taken soon. If there is to be any delay, I certainly hope he will find some way to improve the wages and the working conditions of these men. I am satisfied, however, that in the long run the only satisfactory solution is for these men to come under the direct employ of the Post Office Department.

I suppose the inference to be drawn from the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is that, after all, our employees are not so badly treated, having regard to the fact that he wants these other people that he talked about to become employees of the postal department. I thank him for that nice gesture. I have taken the matter up. I have discussed it with my officials. I might tell the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that all new contracts have in them an escalator clause as to the question of salaries only. With regard to this escalator clause for salaries or wages, we are governed by the prevailing wages that are established by the labour department. As soon as the labour department tells us that the prevailing rate in such a district is so much, we insist upon the contractors passing on to the drivers this addition that we make to our contracts. That clause is in the new contracts. We are now working to get these old contracts-of which

Post Office Act
Winnipeg I think is one-into line with all the others where the escalator will apply.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
1 am glad to know that the matter is toeing given some consideration. I accept the comment that the Postmaster General made as to the inference from my remarks. It is certainly true that post office employees generally are dealt with much better than is this group of employees working under these particular private contractors. There is no question about it that they would be better off directly under the Post Office Department. But I am afraid that the suggestion that seems to be in process of being fulfilled will not solve the problem. This business of having escalator clauses and of referring to the Department of Labour to find out what the prevailing rate is always results in those affected by it lagging far behind. We know that from sad experience.
I am afraid I had better take a minute or two to give some of these figures just to show what is going on. At the present time these men are getting 83 cents an hour, which for a forty-eight hour week works out at less than $40, or around $170 a month. Thomas Jackson Fuel Company pays a starting rate of 85 cents an hour, and that moves up to 90 cents an hour. McCurdy Fuel and Building Supplies pays its truck drivers $1.05 an hour, gives them two weeks holidays with pay and time and a half and double time after certain periods of time for overtime. The rates for those working for the Winnipeg packing plants start at 95 cents an hour and go up after six weeks to $1.11 an hour; average earnings are $52 a week. All of these figures were in effect last July; in some cases they may now be even better. The Coca- Cola Company pays a minimum rate of $55 a week and a maximum rate of $70 a week. The Canadian Pacific Express Company was paying its truck drivers last July a minimum rate of $198.57 a month and a maximum rate of $213.57 a month. The city of Winnipeg pays at one rate only, which is $195 a month. These city employees, employed as truck drivers, get one week's holidays with pay after the first year, two weeks holidays with pay after the second year, and later on that goes up to three weeks holidays with pay, and there are sick leave and other benefits that go with that service. In addition I would point out that civic employees doing comparable work driving trucks get time and a half for overtime and double time if that overtime goes beyond a certain point.
Against that these mail couriers are getting one rate only, 83 cents an hour. They get only one week's holiday with pay, and the only other concession is that there is a little

bit of group insurance, no pension rights or privileges, no sick leave. They do not even get their uniforms; they have to buy them and pay for them themselves. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the minister's reply to the effect that consideration is being given to introducing an escalator clause to all these contracts dealing only with the wage rates does not deal with the problem. I wish he would take what he treated as a compliment to his department a little more seriously than he has thus far, and that he would go the whole way and put these employees directly under his department.

That would mean taking over

About three weeks ago I directed a question to the Postmaster

General with reference to payment for overtime work in the transition period on the inauguration of the new mail deliveries, and was subsequently answered, I think a week later, to the effect that payment for overtime would toe made in cash. Since that time I have been talking to some of the carriers. Perhaps the minister will be good enough to tell me whether the information that I have is correct. I am now told that nothing will be paid until all of these walks have been checked, and that when they have been checked, if it is found that the man has worked six hours overtime a week during the checking period he will then be paid overtime for the period back to the inauguration of the new walk. Is that correct?
That is correct.

What provision is there for the men, some of whose difficulties may be ironed out, and who probably would not show a great volume of overtime at the present time, but who have in the past, in the process of getting the new walk into some kind of efficient working order, put in a great deal of overtime? Are they to get nothing for the time they have put on this work?

As I said this morning in answer I think to a question put to me by the hon. member for Battle River, any walk that can be checked will be paid overtime. But unfortunately, if we are not in a position to check it, there is nothing much we can do about it.

Of course this matter was talked about at great length at the time the changes were made in the deliveries, and these men were working for a couple of months under these conditions, carrying particularly heavy loads and working several hours overtime a day. There are a number of them who have a record in the city of Hamilton, for instance. A record was kept of these hours, and without putting a man actually on with every man every day to check I do not know what figures the department will take to arrive at the amount of overtime that was actually worked, because as conditions changed some of these men left the routes. Some of them have gone on to other jobs, and some of them have had adjustments made so that they are no longer operating under the conditions under which they were operating in March, April and May. There have been a great many hours worked. I quoted some figures in the house at the time I spoke to the minister in the house. I have them here, but I will not
Post Office Act
repeat them at this time. Can some consideration not be given to these men who, everyone will agree, worked many hours overtime in order to inaugurate this new system?

Again I wish to thank the hon. member for the inference that the situation is much better today than it was some weeks ago, because if these couriers are working less time today than they were, then the situation has been corrected to that extent. As to the other feature of the presentation of the hon. member, I am afraid there is nothing much I can do unless an efficient check is made of the routes.

It seems to me the
minister is very quick to put an optimistic slant on any statement made with reference to his department. I would not say the situation is corrected at all. I have a list here showing the overtime worked in the month of April, and for one week of the month of May. At that time, of course, the new routes were in operation, and some of the difficulties had been ironed out; but they are not cured by any means.
I do not think that because a man on a route has been .efficient is any reason for saying that he has not suffered, or that he has not contributed to the efficient operation of a route at considerable cost to himself in both time and effort. I do not think it is proper for the Postmaster General to claim credit for his department for correcting a situation which has been corrected largely as a result of a man's own efforts.
Then, with reference to deliveries, I would say that on previous occasions I asked about the classification of walks as residential walks. Since that time many more complaints have come to me; I would mention one in particular which refers to Main street, Hamilton, within two blocks of the post office proper, which has been classified as a residential walk.
From memory I have made a list of some of the businesses operating in that area. There is the office of a large canning industry, there are several lawyers, a restaurant, a real estate office, a stockbroker, a coal merchant, a large trust company, the main branch of a large bank, the Bell Telephone Company, a hotel and a manufacturing jeweler. Those are only a few of them. Yet that walk is classified as a residential walk, and they have only one mail delivery a day.
Moreover, those who wish to pick up mail at the post office so that they may carry on business more or less in a normal way find that no boxes are available, and that they are unable to do so. It seems to me there should be some way of rectifying a situation

Post Office Act
like that. If the mail delivery service is to be cut, then certainly there should be facilities at the post office whereby these people would be able to pick up their own mail and not have to wait until the afternoon,_ so that banking hours would be over before they received the mail coming to them.
Then there is one other matter I should like to ask about, and that has reference to mail going out from the House of Commons to various parts of the country, and the manner in which it is handled. On Friday, May 25, I wrote a letter here in Ottawa and posted it here in the House of Commons before five o'clock in the afternoon of that day. It was received on the following Tuesday, May 29, in Hamilton. I inquired about this delivery and was told that mail going from the House of Commons and different government departments is handled as second-class mail, and that this accounts for the delay.
If this is not so, then I suggest a check should be made, because apparently that is what has happened; a letter which I posted at five o'clock on Friday was received in Hamilton on the following Tuesday.

I shall most certainly check the latter part of the hon. member's statement. There is absolutely no foundation for the information she was given, namely that it was dealt with as second-class mail. All first-class mail is handled in the same way throughout Canada.
Then, as to residential routes, I have already explained to the committee that they can include as much as twenty-five per cent of commercial or industrial establishments. I have already said to hon. members that a complete re-survey is being made of all commercial and industrial establishments with a view to reorganizing the routes so that if, out of four or five different routes, we can establish a commercial route, we shall do so. But the services of the Post Office Department have to go on. We just cannot stop the machine, make the repairs and then go on after the machine has been repaired. We must make the repairs while the machine operates-and of course that takes a little more time than if it were stopped.
Would a hotel be classified as a residence? Would the Y.M.C.A. or the Y.W.C.A. be classified as residences?

The hon. member is quite
right when she says that about fifteen of the places she named are not residences. But we have to establish a certain standard, and we say that a residential route is one that may include up to twenty-five per cent of commercial or industrial establishments.

I can understand what
the postmaster is driving at, and I would have no quarrel if this were taking place in an outlying area; but when it is right in the very heart of the business district it is entirely different. If the route is being classified as a residential route because of that portion of it lying in a residential part, and removed from the centre of the city, then I urge that the part in the centre of the city should be placed on another route.
That is exactly what we plan doing.
It is a great injustice to these people.

I was glad to hear the Postmaster General say this morning that he realized there had been a good deal of difficulty and confusion in the swing-over in the postal department. I have already expressed my views about most of those things with which I disagree.
The minister said this morning the department was prepared to examine all complaints and to correct any situation where there may be a hardship.
If possible.

Yes, if possible. I believe the minister will recall that he has been receiving a substantial amount of correspondence from the city of Sydney in regard to the business section of that city with a population of from 8,000 to 10,000, and which is three miles away from the main post office. Perhaps the deputy minister will be more familiar with the correspondence. Delivery has been cut to one a day. The city clerk of Sydney has written to me, and I have written to the minister and the deputy minister. To date, the city council are not satisfied with the attitude taken by the department. A letter to me dated May 18 from the clerk of Sydney encloses a copy of a letter written to him by the minister. They say the minister has not faced up to the problem, and they urge that two deliveries a day are necessary in that section. It would mean the addition of only one mail carrier, and this would not entail a very heavy expense. A large area in the city is affected.
I believe the city council of Sydney is making a reasonable request when they ask the minister to relieve the condition by adding another mail carrier to the walk for the purpose of making the additional delivery. I do not know whether the minister has re-examined the problem since he last wrote to the city clerk but, if he has, I would ask him to make a statement. If not,

will he look into the matter again and see if something cannot be done to remedy the situation?

To be perfectly frank, this
is one matter I would have expected to discuss when my estimates are before the committee. I am not ready to give an answer at this time.

Well, I thought I would bring
it to the minister's attention so that he could give some thought to it. I hope the minister will do some more thinking about it, because he will hear more about it.

Mr. Chairman, there is a
veterans housing project in St. John's known as Tunis Court to which there is no mail delivery. Representations have been made to the head postmaster in St. John's but without success. I forwarded a petition signed by these people to the minister on May 4 and he promised he would get in touch with the head postmaster at St. John's. Nothing has been done and the residents are getting anxious.

This is another matter that
should be taken up when the estimates are being considered.

When we were discussing rural
mail routes earlier in the day the minister said he would give me the number of routes that have been suspended temporarily. I wonder if I could have that information broken down into the different provinces. Another matter I have been asked about is the cost of installing lock boxes in post office lobbies. Some people feel that the rates being charged are too high in comparison with the cost of installing them, particularly when other people are being served by mail routes without charge.

When I stated this morning
that I would obtain information for the hon. member for Battle River I meant that I would have that when the estimates were before the committee. The information in the form in which he wants it is being collected. I have nothing before me with regard to the cost of lock boxes, but I shall have that information on my estimates.

Before we drop this matter
of post office boxes may I again direct attention to a matter which I have brought up on other occasions, although not while the present minister was head of the department. In most post offices where lock boxes are installed the outside doors of the post office are locked at six o'clock which creates a hardship for many people who have boxes, particularly those who are in business and
Post Office Act
who cannot get away until after six o'clock. Then again mail may come in by train late in the afternoon or toward the evening, be taken to the post office, distributed to the boxes, but again the outside doors are locked.
Where lock boxes are installed I cannot see any necessity to keep the outside doors locked. The boxes are all locked and the safety of the mail would not be jeopardized if the outside doors were to remain unlocked. When people are paying for their boxes they should have access to them. I join with the hon. member for Battle River in suggesting that the present rates for these boxes are higher than might be charged.

Wherever it is possible we
have what we call a night lobby with direct access from the street. We have these night lobbies in new post offices, but the hon. member will realize that that would not be possible in all post offices.

Most of these post offices are located in general stores and form an important part of the community life.

This again is a matter for my estimates and if possible I should like to keep to the bill. When the estimates are up we will have all the information. In the meantime, I would say to the hon. member for Melfort that the fund stands at present at $300,000.

estimates? I stated this morning that we were closing post offices when it was felt that the rural routes were providing sufficient service. I do not think we could defend keeping a post office open with all the expense necessary to pay the salary of the postmaster, to pay the courier to bring mail from the station to the post office and so on, to serve two, three or four people. I think it is a good policy to close such post offices. As I said this morning, when a mail route is discontinued we will consider the reopening of the post office.

Paragraph (s) reads:
Pay out of postal revenue losses resulting from fire, theft or forgery.
Then subsection 2 is headed "no liability." Those appear to be contradictory. Paragraph (s) is new, and I should like to have the minister explain it.

I have two or three questions, and I do not know whether the minister wants to answer them now or on his estimates. In his report I noticed that last year there were about 44,000 full and parttime employees of the department. Can the minister tell me how many of those were employed through the civil service commission and how many were appointed outside the commission?
I believe that would be a proper question for the estimates.

Would the minister put on record the regulations relative to the hours during which post offices may have their general delivery and other wickets open to serve the public? I find great variations in this regard. For example, in one town the office will be open at a certain hour, and in another town it will be open at a different

hour. In one town the general delivery and other wickets will be closed at noon for an hour and a half or two hours, while in another they will be closed for one hour. In one town they are closed Wednesday afternoons; in another they are closed Thursday afternoons. There must be regulations in connection with this, and I would appreciate it if they could be put on the record.

There seems to be a general impression that service in thinly settled areas and the frequency of the opening of wickets are matters governed solely by the department. Actually attention must be paid to the hours when trains come in, and how frequently the trains run. We have to follow the movement of the trains, and for that reason we cannot draw up any such schedule as the hon. member requested.

close at six or six thirty, and a certain time is allowed after that during which the box holders can get in to get their mail. Is there any set time when the lobby doors must be locked, or is that up to the postmaster?

I do not mean the wicket where they apply for their mail.
The night lobbies will be open only after the post office proper is closed, and the closing of the post office depends upon the arrival of the trains.

I do not think the Postmaster General understands me. Let me take my own post office in Napanee. Our trains come in around noon, at one o'clock and one thirty, and again at midnight. I am trying to find out if there is any set time when the lobby doors must be locked; that is the doors of the building. There are no trains coming in, and I believe the doors are locked at seven or seven thirty.
Under those circumstances the normal closing time would be six o'clock.
That would be for the lobby and all?
Yes.

paragraph (i), subsection 1 of section 5 which gives the postmaster authority to set up stamp vending machines. Some of these stamp vending machines must be making quite a profit, because you have to pay five cents for a four-cent stamp; for three 3-cent stamps, you have to pay ten cents. Theft is no change coming back from these machines. I understand they are established in hotels or wherever they can get a vending machine going.
This leads me back to the fact that you must be paying some commission, or is the machine just paying for its own operation? Paragraph (k) gives the Postmaster General authority to require any person to give security for the due performance of duties performed relative to the Canada Post" Office. Now, I believe that puts my stamp vendor at Charlottetown in the category of a postal employee, at least with regard to his security. I should like some information on that as well.

Post Office Act

As to the first question,
vending machines are established for the convenience of the patrons. They do not get any commission. If my hon. friend has seen one of these machines, he knows that they will give two 2-cent stamps for five cents. They make their commission out of the sale to the public. If the public does not want the convenience of getting two 2-cent stamps for five cents, that is their business, not ours.
On the second question, this paragraph only gives the Postmaster General the authority to ask for security.
Who owns these machines?
The persons operating them, who buy the stamps from us. As to paragraph (k), that only gives the Postmaster General the authority to do that.

I appreciate the answer the Postmaster General gave, and that his answer applied to paragraph (b) of section 5. I should like him to take note now that on the estimates I should like to know how many of those 46,000 employees are permanent.

Paragraph (n) of section 5 gives the Postmaster General authority to establish and alter the limits of postal areas. This gives considerable trouble to any member of parliament who represents a rural constituency, because when the postal department changes an established area we have a great deal of trouble. I should like the Postmaster General to say how he gets the information to establish and alter the limits of certain postal areas that have been in operation for years?

This paragraph (n) has to be read in connection with section 10. Section 10 says:
The rates of postage on letters posted in Canada for delivery in Canada are:

speechtext:
In connection with section 6, there is a comment I should like to make. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: These have always been regulations made exclusively by the Postmaster General, then, without reference to his cabinet colleagues?
That is correct, except (s), of course, which is new.
Paragraph Cd) of section 6 refers to the establishment of rates of postage. Will the Postmaster General bring in his amendment under this paragraph or will he wait until section 11?

Paragraph (d) says: establishing rates of postage on any class of mailable matter for which a rate is not established by this act;
Section 11 does establish a rate, and therefore this paragraph excludes section 11.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Unlawful use of mails.

Will the Postmaster General explain just what types of tickets for raffles and so on are prohibited? Where is the line drawn? I received a few tickets through the mail from one organization, and printed on the tickets were the words "Cleared for the purpose of complying with the law". Some really responsible people have been denied the use of the mails. Where is the line drawn?
The Criminal Code, I am afraid.

Would the minister mind
explaining the sections of the Criminal Code covering lottery tickets?
There are a number of sections in the Criminal Code covering these various matters.
There are communities that are building community halls or war memorials, and some very responsible people have been denied the use of the mail by a ruling of the Postmaster General.

I am afraid it will have to continue to be like that. Tickets for all drawings that go through the mail, whether

they call them lotteries, bingos or anything else, for prizes worth more than $50, come within the classification of a lottery. They are denied the use of the mails. I understand that by doing so we are hitting quite a number of charitable institutions that we should be helping. But on the other hand, if we allow one of these charitable institutions to go through the mails, we will be flooded by a hundred rackets that should not go through the mails.

Subsection 2 of section 7 provides for the setting up of a board of review nominated by the Postmaster General. Has the Postmaster General received any representations from public bodies asking that that board of review should be independent instead of being nominated by the Postmaster General?
I received some representation to that effect from the board of trade of the city of Toronto, yes.
Has the minister given any consideration to that request?

I have given it consideration and I have discussed it with the officials of the department. Any independent board that might be nominated under the suggestion of the Toronto board of trade would, I suppose, be one board like the railway board or the air transport board or ones like that, which would again be a governmental body. It is felt that the authority should be left in the discretion of the Postmaster General.
Last year when this matter was broached, the request that was made of the department was not so much to have an independent board as to give the persons whose mail had been stopped an opportunity of explaining to somebody in the department the reasons why it should not be stopped. Last year I promised that this would be done. By introducing section 7 we are just giving effect to the promise that was made last year.

For his own protection and in order to avoid criticism, would the minister not be well advised to make that an independent board? To me there does not seem to be any difference between appealing to the Postmaster General and appealing to a board appointed by the Postmaster General. To me that seems to be one and the same thing. I would strongly urge that consideration be given to the suggestion to which I have referred.
Then there was another request to the effect that there should be the normal right of appeal to the courts from ministerial action
Post Office Act
based upon the findings of a board of review. Has the minister given consideration to that question?

That is so. The brief of the board of trade of the city of Toronto also mentions the question of an appeal; but it was not felt that the discretion should be taken away from the Postmaster General. I realize that it is quite a heavy responsibility, but I think it is one that a minister of the crown should be ready to accept.

I should like to say a word or two about the wording of section 8 (1). I understand as well as anyone else what this wording is intended to mean. I realize that we are following a practice that has come down as a bit of tradition. Except as provided in subsection two, the Postmaster General has the sole and exclusive privilege of collecting, conveying and delivering letters within Canada.
The Postmaster General is a fairly capable fellow, but he is not as ubiquitous as that. I do not think we should have on our statute books a statute which seems to say that, as to every letter that is picked up anywhere in Canada, or any letter that is delivered, it is done by the Postmaster General.
Not himself.

speechtext:
If the hon. member had been
at law school, he would know different.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs refers to law school. That is exactly my point. Professional lawyers do not stop to look at the meaning of the language they have been using-

it; that is why.

They do not look at the meaning of the language they have been using across the years. We all know that what is meant by this section is the Post Office Department or the Canada Post Office. In fact, back in section 2 (1) (a) we have defined Canada Post Office in these words:

Then a little later on we had section 3 which provided for the organization of a department to be known as the Post Office

Department over which the Postmaster General is to preside. But it seems to me that we should be realistic and factual in our wording, and that in a section like this, instead of saying that the Postmaster General collects, conveys and delivers all letters within Canada, we should say either the Post Office Department or the Canada Post Office. I like that phrase that has come into this act; I refer to the "Canada Post Office". I think it would be preferable if in this section the wording had been:

It is not a matter that is of sufficient importance for me to bother to move an amendment. But I suggest the idea seriously, not just in fun. I think the wording in our statutes should conform to the facts of the situation.

The same wording has been
in the act since 1867.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That is exactly the point
and that is exactly the trouble. Certainly it has been there since 1867. I realize that. In the notes to the right it says that this section has been section 35, and that means no change has been made. That was good Victorian legal language back in 1867, but we do not mean that today. We do not mean that our good friend Edouard Rinfret is going to run around, collect all the letters and deliver them himself. Then why say that? We mean the department over which he presides. I think a change should be made. In fact, to bring the matter to a head, I will, despite what I said a moment ago, offer an amendment. I move:
That section 8(1) be amended by deleting therefrom the words "Postmaster General" and by substituting therefor the words "Canada Post Office."

There has been quite a lot of discussion on this subject. One matter that has been brought up is whether or not the amount of $12 million which was paid last year in services was or was not a subsidy. I beg leave to disagree with the leader of the opposition, and I am very fortunate in having Webster on my side. The New International dictionary says a subsidy is:
A grant of funds or property from a government, as of the state or municipal corporation, to a private person or company to assist in the establishment or support of an enterprise deemed advantageous to the public; a subvention. In practice subsidies are chiefly granted in aid of transportation enterprises, as to ship, canal, air transport, or railway companies, bounties on sugar being next in importance. A subsidy may be a simple gift or may consist in the payment of an amount in excess of the usual charges for any service, as in carrying the mails, or of funds to aid in establishing or maintaining a service or equipment larger or more powerful than the state of trade would warrant, as the building and keeping in service of vessels designed for use as cruisers and auxiliaries in war.
According to Webster the excess of what the Post Office Department has to pay for transportation on newspapers over what we actually receive would therefore be a subsidy. Therefore last year we gave a subsidy of $12 million to newspapers and magazines. Newspapers will claim that it was not paid to them directly. That may be true. They may have been paid for the purpose of the rural readers. That also may be true. It also remains true, Mr. Chairman, that never has any government given for the purpose an amount as large as the one that we did give last year, to wit, $12 million, and the rural readers have benefited to that extent. The year before the subsidy was $11 million; the year before that the subsidy was $11 million. It has kept on increasing all the time. It is felt that at some time or other, with the mounting costs that we have to bear in the department, something has to be done to bring the matter a little more in line with the situation. With the estimate that we have at the present time, the present year in which we are now engaged, unless there is some change, will bring us a deficit of some $14 million or $15 million on the second-class category alone.
I have already said that if we did not have a deficit we could reduce the postage throughout the four-cent rate area so as to bring it into conformity with other areas in Canada so that we could have a uniform rate of 3 cents throughout the country. But the surplus that we have on the first-class mail we have to apply to certain deficits that we have on certain other classes. I have already spoken of the $12 million deficit on the second-class mail. I have also referred, prior

Post Office Act
to this debate, to the deficit of $2,250,000 that we have on third-class matter. The rate there has been adjusted. I have also referred to a deficit of $1,800,000 that we had on registration. That rate has been adjusted upwards. In all the various compartments where we had deficits we have tried to bring them in line with expenditures. In this instance, Mr. Chairman, we have a deficit of $12 million, and we are seeking from the newspapers only one-sixth of the amount, to wit, $2 million.
Some representations have been made to the effect that we have discriminated against certain classes of second-class matter. I should like to point out that last year the Post Office Department carried 158,004,560 pounds of mail. Out of this total, 66,355,674 were carried for dailies over 10,000 circulation and 3,480,407 for dailies under 10,000. A weight of 70 million pounds was carried for dailies, as against all the rest of the second-class matter.
Therefore the situation is that if we are to ask the people of Canada to pay two million dollars more in postal rates we have to divide the field in two, having on one side all the dailies, and on the other the weeklies, the monthlies, the quarterlies and all the others. That is the division made in the weight. After all, weight is what we have to reckon with. What we have to charge for is a service we give, and the service we give must be reckoned on the poundage we have to move.
Therefore in the department we have made a calculation of the various ways of making a separation between these two bodies. We figure that one million dollars should come out of dailies and one million dollars should come from the rest of the field. We have arranged our rates so that it would produce exactly that amount.

I do not wish to interrupt the Postmaster General, but when he says that one million dollars is to come out of the dailies, and another million from the rest of the papers, does he mean by that that the computation he now makes provides that there will be one million dollars paid in respect of the carrying of the daily papers and one million dollars in respect of other types of material carried in this way?

That is right. That would
be only the increase, of course. The accusation of discrimination has been mentioned in respect of the various rates charged. There again I would point out to the committee that, in assessing rates for various newspapers or periodicals,

we must take into consideration the strain being put on the post office by these various papers.
Dailies of over 10,000 circulation entail the highest cost of any class of publication. Many railway post offices could be discontinued if no dailies were in existence. The daily newspapers have to receive top priority at peak work-load periods.'

There might be a lot of
institutions which would have to close if we did not have the daily papers.

One thing I am sure of is that I would not have a $12 million deficit, and I could pass that on to the rest of the population of Canada. The dailies come to the post office when the big rush is on. We must give them a priority, because they do not want to be delayed, nor do we want to delay them. They have to be on the market as soon as possible. With the weeklies and monthlies, on the other hand, the question of reaching the market one or two hours later is not of such great importance. Therefore, instead of handling this business at a time of peak load, we can deal with the weeklies and monthlies one or two hours later, when the rush is over.
Another question which arises in connection with the big dailies, and one which involves another strain upon us, is the fact that they are put to mail in the post offices which are the most expensive for us to operate.
I have before me the various considerations as they affect the dailies, the tri-weeklies, the semi-weeklies and the weeklies, the monthlies, the fortnightlies and the quarterlies. It must be realized that a monthly magazine comes to us only once a month, whereas a daily comes twenty-five times a month. We have to deal with the papers as they come to the office.
However, I believe the real test lies in the weights I have indicated, which show that the dailies, by themselves, constitute half the total weight we have to carry. Information has been put on record indicating what these increased rates would mean to rural mail readers. I believe it was the leader of the opposition who read into Hansard a computation he had made to show increases for those readers. I come back to the fact that there is one way in which added revenue could be obtained, and in the process of obtaining it the postal department would be doing something of very great advantage to the people of Canada, and that is, to place really high postal rates on crime comics, sex magazines and trash of that kind, which no Canadian

parent wants to see coming into his house if he can possibly avoid it. I do not think for one moment that the Postmaster General believes that the newspapers across this country are going to absorb the increased postal rates involved in whatever amendments may be adopted. By virtue of the fact that a substantial part of their space is devoted to revenue earning advertising, undoubtedly the newspapers will charge some of the increase to that advertising. I am not in a position to say how it would work out; but one thing I am sure of is that in this or any other business the added cost is going to be added to the price ultimately charged for that thing the people are buying. This applies whether it is a newspaper, a pair of shoes, an automobile or a food item.
It would be well if we got away from the suggestion that provisions of this kind are simply subsidies for the newspapers which the people, after all, buy for purposes of reading.
While every appropriate measure should be taken to place our public services on a businesslike basis, it can only come with some measure of surprise that a postal rate which has stood so long at the figure which has been on the statute books should require suddenly to be raised to the extent it is now being raised in the amendment before us.
The Postmaster General has referred to the United States, and what is being done over there. I would point out that if in the United States they go ahead to provide increases, such as the Postmaster General has suggested are likely, it has been indicated that those increases will not be made at one time, but that they will be made in three stages. Mr. Chairman, before this section carries I should like to make a few comments with respect to it, and also I would have them apply to section 23. I am interested in these amendments to the Post

Office Act. However, I was sorry to find, upon reading the bill, that it did not make any provision which in my opinion was satisfactory for the settlement of the problem with respect to rural mail couriers of Canada.
My constituency of Lambton-Kent is typical, I believe, of those in western Ontario, in that it has many rural mail contracts. I believe that all told there are seventy mail routes in the constituency, with ten stage services, or probably eighty all told. Throughout Canada I believe there are about 5,200 rural mail contracts, in addition to some 7,500 stage and side service contracts. These refer to services from one post office to another, or from railway depots to post offices.
The average price paid for rural mail routes throughout Canada is $53.30 per mile per year, or pretty close to $54. The contracts in operation in the constituency of Lambton-Kent run at approximately $54, so that in that constituency they are almost the same as the average across the country. These mail contracts have been let for years under a system of public tenders, in which four-year contracts are awarded. The contract is renewed at the end of four years without calling for public tender if the courier is willing to continue the service at the same rate and if there is no serious objection to the service being given. This practice has been in operation for a long time.
Between 1945 and 1947 the cost of operating rural mail services increased along with the general cost of living. In March 1947 a special act of parliament was enacted which provided for the bonusing or subsidizing of mail contracts then in force. This was called, the Mail Contracts Supplemental Payments Act. That act was in operation for one year and then was extended for another year, so it was in operation from 1947 to 1949. Many of these contracts had previously been awarded at ridiculously low rates and they were adjusted to take care of the increased cost of operation. The new price was agreed upon between the post office officials and the contractor.
I would think that during those two years approximately 90 per cent of all the rural mail contracts in Canada were adjusted. When those contracts had expired at the end of four years of operation the subsidies or bonuses were incorporated in the new contracts. The new contracts provided for a larger remuneration than had been agreed to when the tenders were accepted. I think it is generally accepted among the rural mail contractors that that was one of the

best moves that had been made in many years on behalf of the rural mail couriers.
It provided an equalization in the amounts received by rural mail couriers who were working out of the same post office.
I contend that the remuneration now paid to rural mail contractors was not arrived at by means of public tenders. These rates were arrived at by the post office officials. Section 23 permits the awarding of contracts for $1,000 or less without calling for public tenders. I am quite satisfied that sections 22 and 23 do not clarify the situation. They make things a lot more difficult in the way of administration than they were before. I am quite syre that in my own riding of Lambton-Kent this section 23 will not affect five per cent of the contractors, and I am quite sure that is true of the rest of the dominion. Only those with very short routes will be helped by this new regulation.
I have received many letters from rural mail contractors stating that they cannot carry on under the present rates as costs have gone up greatly since 1949. Many of these men want to quit. Five mail routes operate out of the town of Bothwell. Quite recently one route was put up for tender and was awarded to the lowest bidder at approximately $70 per mile. The other four routes operating from the same post office receive approximately $50 per mile. If rural mail contractors decide that they are going to give up their old contracts in an effort to get new ones, tenders will have to be called and new contracts made out. In my opinion that would cost the department a great deal more than would the re-enacting of the Mail Contracts Supplemental Payments Act.
I urge the Post Office Department to consider re-enacting that act, because it would be most satisfactory to the rural mail couriers. I know it will probably be said that if that is done there will be a lot of patronage, but candidly I do not believe that would be true. I know of no patronage in Lambton-Kent in the past several years in connection with the awarding of mail contracts. These contracts have been awarded and renewed and adjusted by the Post Office Department. There were no reactions during the time the Mail Contracts Supplemental Payments Act was in operation and I had no complaints that patronage was being practised in any way.
Section 26 provides that bids may be got from anywhere at all. This matter will probably be dealt with under the next section. I contend that the public tender system in connection with rural mail routes is antiquated and should be liquidated. If that
Post Office Act
were done we would not have the difficulties we have now in awarding contracts. Most people handling His Majesty's mail are on a salary basis. This is true of all letter carriers. Then why not rural mail couriers?
The rural mail system was established in 1908, the first service being from Ancaster to Hamilton. In 1909 it was put into general operation all over Canada. Conditions have changed greatly. Let us bring this matter up to date and adjust these contracts so that they will meet the present cost of operation. Then these people should be put under the civil service or on some permanent basis. If that were done we would not need to go through this process from year to year.
Rural mail delivery should be extended to all rural residents in Canada. There is a lot of free franking and I would suggest that we do something to curtail that and extend rural mail delivery to all rural residents in Canada. It would not cost much more and, as someone has said, the post office service contributes considerably to our social and economic development. It should not be curtailed in any way.
I urge again the Post Office Department to re-enact the Mail Contracts Supplemental Payments Act. It worked well before and it will work well again and in the end will give us better service and cost the Post Office Department and the taxpayers a lot less to run.

I think there is one piece of information the committee should have if we are to intelligently discuss the advisability of adopting this section. As you know, Mr. Chairman, this provides that the Postmaster General may make a contract for rural mail carriage where the amount of the contract is $1,000 or less. In addition to the number of those contracts I would like to know what percentage that number is of the total contracts for rural mail carriage throughout Canada.

That would represent about
70 per cent in number and 32 per cent in value.

Then may I ask another question which has been suggested by the hon. member for Cumberland. How many rural mail contracts are there in Canada?

As of March 31, 1951, there were 5,087. On the point raised by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent concerning increases to contractors, as the hon. member has said the effect of the supplemental payments act was that about 80 per cent of all mail contractors had received adjustments prior to March 31, 1949. In order to see whether the time had come to put a similar act in operation we made a calculation of the percentage increase that had taken place from April 1, 1949, to date. We discovered that in 1946, when the supplemental payments act was put into operation, there had been an increase of 37 per cent in the previous year. On the other hand we discovered that from April 1, 1949, to date the increase on proportionate tenders and proportionate routes has been only 17 per cent. I can assure the house that the department is keeping closely in touch with the situation, and if this percentage increase reaches any greater proportions no doubt we will have something to present to the house in the fall if necessary.
Has the minister invited the suggestions or opinions of the organized mail couriers with respect to this amendment, and are they satisfied with it?

There is only one other point I would like cleared up. When the Postmaster General said this $1,000 provision would affect 70 per cent of the rural mail contracts, surely he was also taking into account all these side services, the short routes such as those from railway depots to post offices, stagecoaches, and so on.
