Some time ago I placed on the order paper a resolution having to do with mail couriers which was not reached owing to the passage of time, so I should like to say a word now. I agree with others who have spoken that some changes should be made in the remuneration of our mail couriers.

I do not want to take too much of the time of the house, but I should like briefly to go over the points set out in my resolution.
My idea was to place all mail couriers on the same basis, that of a permanent rate per mile. Since all mail couriers are performing identical services for the Post Office Department, I submit they should be placed upon the basis of equality, not only as between themselves but in comparison with other employees doing similar work for the government. This would eliminate the existing vagaries in the practice of tendering for contracts, which make every tender a competition. Often accepted tenders are so low that the contractors cannot make a living, with the result that the bondsmen must perform the service for one year before the contracts can be terminated.
My next point simply provided that the basic rate should be the present average rate. The next point was that the permanent rate should become effective on the expiration of the existing contracts. This would permit all existing contracts to terminate in accordance with their specified terms. My fourth point provided for an increase of 10 per cent.
I would not insist upon that in any regulation the department might see fit to adopt.
I would rather change that now to an increase over the average rate per mile now being received.
Many couriers have asked me to seek increases for them. They claim that their living costs have increased, together with the cost of equipment necessary to perform the service. I have had to tell them that no increases have been granted since March, 1949, on the termination of the supplemental benefits. The percentage increase would be a reasonable request, since the employees of all other departments have had their salaries increased. In my opinion there are far better grounds for increasing the rate of pay of the rural courier, who in performance of his duties must face the elements six days a week, and in the spring and fall often has to drive over very bad roads in stormy weather. In contrast to this, those employed in other departments have much shorter hours and perform their duties in well furnished and heated offices. This government has made successful efforts to deal with inequalities as they have appeared in our industrial and economic life. My sole purpose in rising was to bring to the attention of the government, in the most forceful way I could, the need for some adjustment. The purpose of the resolution was to bring to the attention of the government existing inequalities in the rural mail courier service itself, and to enable us to compare the insecurity

of the rural mail couriers with the security of other groups of employees engaged by the Post Office Department, who are afforded the security of sick benefits, pensions on retirement, yearly vacations with pay, while the rural mail courier is left to bargain with the department individually on unequal terms.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I feel quite strongly on this subject. Since I have become a member of this parliament I have had many requests on different occasions, and I have written to the Postmaster General directly. While the replies were always courteous and polite, nevertheless under our present act we could receive no relief for our mail couriers. There are many rural areas, Mr. Chairman, in which we are unable to provide daily mail service for the residents because of the regulation that there must be a minimum of four boxholders to the mile. I should like to see a change made in this regulation so that our farmers, fishermen, miners, lumbermen, the producers of our national wealth, would be placed on an equal footing with the urban dwellers in Canada. I am urging the minister to give this matter serious consideration. I believe the time has now arrived when a change should be made. It is difficult to convince the rural mail couriers who are serving the people of Canada honestly and well, often at great risk to their physical welfare, that now is an opportune time, when the Postmaster General is making some changes, to have these requests met.

Mr. Chairman, I notice there is a considerable change in the wording of this section from the old section 73 from which it has been derived. I believe the Postmaster General had a discretion before, but there was a provision which put an onus upon him. He could only conclude such contracts in special cases by private agreement when he conceived the public interest would be protected by such a course. I notice that those words have been omitted, and the Postmaster General has been given a free hand to make such contracts without any such binding stipulations as the old section contained. I should like the Postmaster General to tell us how he proposes to enter into contracts which are under $1,000. Will he proceed in the same manner as he does now for those under $200? Can he give us any idea of the routine which will be followed?

We shall proceed in exactly the same way as we are doing now for contracts under $200. As hon. members of the house will know, in awarding these contracts the Postmaster General is obliged to follow the amount ordinarily paid for services of a like nature under contracts made after inviting 80709-251
Post Office Act
tenders. There is a condition attached to this section which makes it compulsory for the Postmaster General and his employees , to follow the trend of the tenders, as we are doing now for contracts below $200.

Can you
describe how you are doing that now?

We are asking persons to submit offers, we do not call them tenders, and when they are reasonable we do accept them. If they are not reasonable we reject them and go after some other offers.
I believe I have already dealt with the question raised by the hon. member for Kings. If we were to establish some sort of average throughout the country for rural mail couriers, we would have an extraordinary situation. People who are now above the average would be reduced to the average, whereas others who are below the average would be elevated to it. There is a special reason why some couriers are below the average. It is because their route is not as long; there might not be as many boxes; the hours of service might be different; the conditions of the road might be different; the general climatic conditions might be different; and the degree of competition might be different. All those questions have some influence on the amount of the tender. If we have an easy contract that can be performed for say $49, and on the other hand we have another contract covering difficult conditions making a tender of $71 necessary, the person that is contracting at $71 would be punished very severely if we were to make some sort of average between those two. The one having the contract at $49 per mile would benefit to a great extent for performing these services.
There was one other question which I should like to answer. We calculate that since 1946 the average prices for rural mail couriers have increased by about 30 per cent.

I wish to make a remark on these two sections. We are dealing with section 22, but section 23 is also involved to some extent. I understand that the minister and the department are having great difficulty, in some instances, in getting people to take contracts at current levels. I quite agree that often the tenders are of such a nature that the person who has a tender accepted is in reality performing a service for an amount far below what the service is worth. That should be remedied.
I just want to point out that, taking these two sections together, it really means that henceforth the Postmaster General will be able to award contracts of $1,000 or less without a tender. It seems to me that this is going

Post Office Act
back instead of going forward. What we are doing is opening the door once again to more of the patronage system. Ever since the first war the disposition of this house has been to get away from the patronage system. I believe that if a contract involving $1,000 is to be awarded, then it should be properly advertised and tenders invited. I do not say that the Postmaster General or the department should always accept the lowest tender, but I think the ability of the person tendering to perform the contract has to be considered. I think that this is opening wider a door that this parliament has tried to close for a good many years, namely the door of patronage. I personally think that it would be better to leave the act as it now is and to say that any contract in an amount of over $200 should be advertised and that tenders should be called. I think that would be much more satisfactory to the house, even if we expected the Postmaster General at times perhaps to award a contract to one who was not necessarily the lowest tenderer. But I personally think that we have tried in the House of Commons to get away from the patronage system; yet here we are once again opening the door a little wider than it has been in the past. I should like to see the old amount restored in this particular clause. Just to test the feeling of the committee on this matter, I am going to move:
That clause 22 be amended by deleting the words "more than one thousand dollars" and by substituting instead thereof the words "more than two hundred dollars."
That really has the effect of restoring the act to its original form. I think we are unwise to open wide a door that we have been trying to close in this parliament over the years. I know that objection may be raised that there is something like cutthroat competition, which means that the couriers often take contracts for far less than the service is worth. But at the same time I think we in this parliament are wise to try to get away from patronage as much as we can.

I was going to ask the
minister a question in connection with subsection 1 of section 23. The procedure that was outlined by the Postmaster General, in answer to the inquiry of the hon. member for St. John's West, did not seem to me to be any too clear. It is perhaps my fault that that condition arose but, if I may, I should like to have the minister's assistance on the point. What actually is the procedure under that section, having in mind a comparable arrangement made previously under the $200 ceiling? First of all, the minister said, of course, that he invites offers. But
fMr. Coldwell.l
I am greatly interested in knowing what kind of invitation is extended to these privileged people and, second, what the form of the invitation is when it is so extended to them. Those are the two things that I think are important at this stage.

The mail has to go through.
We have inspectors in the districts and we have postmasters in the districts, and they make inquiries from the persons who might be interested-such as taxi drivers or others -or who could be interested, and they endeavour to obtain from those people some offer to do the job. The offer is then referred to our department of communications here, which looks it over. If the offer is reasonable and if it is in keeping with the prices prevailing for similar contracts of like nature where a tender is called, then it is accepted. But if it is out of all proportion in comparison with contracts where tenders are called, then we do not accept it at all.
As to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, when the act was originally passed in 1867 the amount of $200 represented 86-9 per cent of the contracts. The value of money has increased considerably; I think fivefold is not saying too much.
Careful.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It has decreased, you mean.

The value of money has
decreased.

The value of money has
decreased to a fifth of its former value. I think that $1,000 today represents approximately the same value as $200 in 1867. I now found that under the $200 clause only 17 per cent of the contracts are covered.
As to the other suggestion, that for those contracts below $1,000 we could ask for tenders and not accept the lowest, I think that would make a farce of the tender system. Under section 24 the Postmaster General is obliged to accept the lowest tenderer who offers sufficient security for the faithful performance of the contract. We therefore could not have one system of tenders for one class and another set of tenders for another class.

Does not that phrase allow you some latitude even now? The section reads in part:
. . . the contract shall be awarded to the lowest tenderer who has offered sufficient security for the faithful performance of the contract . . .
That does not mean financial security only.
It does to a certain extent.
Yes, to a certain extent.

For instance, we would not accept a drunkard as offering sufficient security. We would not accept as offering sufficient security one of our old contractors who had been dismissed for not performing his duties satisfactorily. There are also some other instances like that. For instance, there are the big contracts where a contractor must have quite heavy equipment. If a person is not sufficiently well off financially he could not, of course, offer sufficient security.

I know of cases where the lowest tenderer has not been accepted. I know of quite a few cases in rural districts where the lowest tender was considered too high and the route was closed. Under this clause 24 it would appear that they must accept the lowest tenderer.
On that question I would refer the hon. member to section 26.

May I ask the minister whether the department has any objection to reletting a contract that has expired now or during the past few months, if they get a price approximately 17 per cent higher than the old contract price? The minister told us that the increase has been, on an average, approximately 17 per cent since April 1, 1949. In many cases I believe the contracts expiring now have been of a duration of four years. I wonder whether any objection is taken to letting the contract again to the old contractor for about 17 per cent, 18 per cent or 20 per cent above the old contract price.
Under the new system, if the contract is below $1,000 I suppose that would be possible. If the contract is over $1,000, I do not think it would be possible; we would have to call new tenders.

I understand that perfectly. But in cases where tenders have been called, and where there have been one, two or three tenderers, I wonder whether there is any objection to letting the contract at approximately 17 per cent to 20 per cent above the old contract price. That is what I was trying to get at, and whether that procedure applies all over Canada or just to some sections.

As I said before, the average price or the price tag for a route is fairly well fixed up in the minds of our employees. Of course, they have had to revise some of their figures; but as far as tenders go they know now approximately what a route should call for.
Post Office Act
I know the officials have got things in their heads; I think some of these should be moved out. That is what I am complaining about.

I know they are tough
bargainers.
I am trying to get service for people in rural communities, because I think they are the most important people in the country.

At the present time under the existing set-up there is no authority for the Postmaster General to continue a contract except on exactly the same terms as the old contract, provided that he is satisfied the service has been satisfactory. Under the new system, as I said before, if the contract is below $1,000 there will be the possibility of revision, and when the clause passes it is my intention to deal with each of these cases; but over $1,000 there is still no authority in this bill by which I can do what the hon. member suggests.

I will make it a little more specific in order to get a specific answer. A man took a contract four years ago. It was for $500. The contract has now expired. The contractor wants an increase of $100 over what he previously tendered for. What will the Postmaster General do in that case when there is only one tender received?
At the present time, and until this clause carries, there is absolutely nothing I can do for him.
When the clause carries, what then?

Then I suppose the contractor will have to give us three months' notice of cancellation of his contract. We will reexamine the matter, and we hope to be able to arrive at some mutually satisfactory figure.

You have already fired him. He does not need to give notice. I am trying to get service. We had at least two country post offices that were closed when we were given rural mail service. This is my complaint. We had the post offices, which were closed, and we were given rural mail service. Now you have stopped the rural mail service because the man wants another $100.
I did not say that. I said we would probably come to a mutually satisfactory solution.
I will come to see the minister in a very short time.

Does the Postmaster General think that he is going to take on that responsibility? It would be

Post Office Act
very difficult for him to attend to thousands of contracts. He will not be able to do that.
During the war under the supplemental payments act a hundred per cent of these contracts were covered, and yet the department was able to handle it.
That is what I was going to suggest. You should devise some regulations of a general nature and not leave it to a rule of thumb to be handled in each case.

I suppose the regulations will be developed as time goes on. I am not 'going to deal with every one of them personally. The section says that the Postmaster [DOT]General may enter into contracts. It will be the officials of the department who will do that.

I am interested in seeing that the people get fair play. There is a great deal of suspicion that political patronage plays some part in the giving of these contracts. I would like the Postmaster General to have it so that he would be above suspicion.

There was absolutely no suspicion during the war while the supplemental payments act was in operation. I think it is only fair to say that the officials of the department conducted this without looking at any colours and they arranged the various contracts according to the merits of the application.

Why is the
minister referring to what happened during the war? The war has been over for six years.
Because during the war we had exactly the same situation, and we were-
How?

We had the supplemental
payments act under which payments were made to rural couriers. That was in operation from 1946 to March 31, 1949, under under which any courier could apply to the department for an increase, and the department would look at the figures to see whether an increase was justified; and if the increase was warranted the department would grant it. The power is the same today as it was then.
Is that act in force now?
No.

Why is the
minister bringing it up?
[Mr. Browne (St. John's West) .1

The principle is the same
today as it was then. If the officials of the department were able to look at the various contracts on their merits at that time, they are the same officials that are here today, and is there any reason to suspect that they would not do it today as they did it then?

I just want to support
what the Postmaster General has said with reference to the years 1947 to 1949. I quite appreciate, and I am sure the departmental officials appreciate, that it is rather difficult to set a basic pay, because you have different lengths of routes, you have different numbers of boxes on the routes, and you have different conditions of routes. That is quite true, but the fact remains that from March, 1947, to March, 1949, it was in operation; it did give good satisfaction, and if you do not believe me ask the 2,500 rural mail couriers.

The minister spoke about
the regulations and the legislation known as the supplemental payments legislation. There was one grave objection to that from the standpoint of procedure, namely, that it unnecessarily tied the hands of the officials of the Post Office Department. What happened' was this. No real publicity was given to the fact that these supplemental payments were available to the rural mail couriers. There are hundreds of rural mail couriers across Canada who did not know that there was a supplemental payment made or available. So bad was the situation at one time that I decided to write to all my rural mail couriers and tell them it was available. Immediately I got a great number of replies, and in all fairness to the officials of the department I must say that in most instances they received reasonable compensation for the amount that they should have received. But that did not cure the situation at all, because after the faces of the rural mail couriers had been ground down under this kind of legislation, which calls for the tender system, surely it was only fair that they should have been told by the government in some way or other that they were entitled to these bonuses if they applied for them.
To make matters worse, after a certain length of time had expired the law cut them off altogether from making an application for the bonus. If you were to take a census of the rural mail couriers for the last five years in Canada I fancy you would find a lot of people to whom the government owed money if the government had only allowed them to know that there was money coming to them if they made an application

for it. That is not a criticism of the officials of the department; it is a criticism of government policy that I think is inexcusable, and it was a shameful exhibition at the time in which it was done.
I only want to say this to the minister in connection with section 23. I realize his difficulties in connection with it, but I know that he has probably got in his mind the fact that if the tender system is removed -by the way it is only removed at the option of the government; it is not removed at the option of the individual. The government has held the trump cards ever since it was started, and they are continuing to do so. So long as they sit as a government they are going to be able to put their finger on a man in any section where they may want to have a rural mail courier, and no one will be able to do anything about it. On the other hand, if the government does not think the right person is doing the work, or if it thinks some change should be made, then it is free to open it up for tender. I can see, and I am sure other members in the committee must be able to see, that this opens the door to a condition of patronage I know no member is anxious to see in Canada.
I do wish to say that I am sorry there is not some provision which would be helpful in the act. If we are going to open up what looks like a patronage section and if we are going back to the dark ages in politics in connection with the appointment of rural mail couriers, then, in his own defence, I think the minister should have some provision in the act. He should have some kind of protection with respect to the awarding of these contracts. To my mind, it would appear to be a big responsibility because where patronage is not involved at all he will be suspected of patronage-and I do not want to have any such suspicion fall upon the minister.
How kind of you!

If we are going to have a reversal to a medieval system of contracting, then, if it cannot be done out in the open while the contract is made, it certainly should be out in the open as soon as it is made. While post-mortems are not a great help, sometimes they save mistakes in the future.
I have no doubt the government is determined that this section shall pass, and undoubtedly the amendment offered by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar will not receive unanimous support from the government benches. It would have to have that support if it were to pass.
Post Office Act
When contracts are awarded, how are we going to know each year when we comeback to the session of parliament? Will there-be a special report laid on the table of the-house dealing with these contracts awarded; behind closed doors, shall I say? Will we-have the door opened in this way so that we will know what went on when these-contracts were entered into? I suggest parliament is entitled to have that. It is only a fair and reasonable suggestion to make, and I suggest to the minister that it should be done.
I would close by stating that I am sure the-minister knows, as do other hon. members in the committee, that I have been pretty faithful and persistent in my advocacy of a committee to deal with that part of the-legislation dealing with rural mail couriers, as well as other parts of it. I believe when we come to assess the time taken up in this session in discussing amendments to the Post Office Act the government will have to accept a large measure of responsibility for the fact that the bill was not allowed to go to a special committee of the house, where it could have been dealt with. In view of the fact that this is the first amending bill since 1867, so far as this act is concerned, it seems to me there should have been an opportunity for much more debate and discussion than we are now given. I am more certain in my mind now that I was right when I asked for a committee than I was when I originally asked for it.

Replying to the hon. member I would say that while at the beginning it might have been true that many of the couriers did not know about the existence of the supplementary act, at the end 80 per cent of them were taken care of through an increase made by the officials.
Then, as to the hon. member's second question, I would reply that at the present time there is no procedure for tabling in the house the names of contractors under the' tendering system. But when hon. members wish to place questions on the order paper they are free to do so, and I see no reason why that procedure should not be continued.

Mr. Chairman, I have one further comment to make. My understanding is that there was a special act of parliament in 1947 which provided a supplement for mail couriers, and that it passed through this-House of Commons. All members knew about it; and I am amazed to think that the hon. member for Peel did not know about it. If hon. members did not tell the post office authorities and have them tell the couriers,, then they were not on to their jobs.

Post Office Act

I suggest the gratuitous lecture which has been read to some of us by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent must have been directed to someone other than myself. However, I do hasten to assure the committee that the great difficulty did not arise after the act was finally passed. If my memory serves me correctly, some of the greatest difficulties arose through the legislation by order in council under which the provision was originally instituted. When it was made in 1947, it came as part of legislation that was then being passed to take the place of order-in-council legislation of previous years. We had asked the government time and again to make these orders in council more public than they had been made. The rural mail couriers did not hear about it, and I think my hon. friend must bear some share of responsibility for that.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to enter into any controversy which would hold up the passage of the bill. On another occasion, when we were discussing another section, I was ruled out of order when the subject of patronage was mentioned. However, I was surprised this evening to hear the leader of the C.C.F. attack the government and then move an amendment on the ground of changing from the $200 jobs, which existed when money was worth much more than it is now, to thousand-dollar jobs for hauling mail. In this way he has brought in the matter of patronage.
Well, I do not think I have the right this evening to go into the history of the C.C.F., so far as patronage is concerned. I would point out to the hon. member who has offered the amendment that, in so far as the Post Office Department is concerned, there are older Liberal members than I am in the House of Commons who no longer make recommendations to the Post Office Department, because they say those recommendations are never acted upon. So, as for patronage being practised in the Post Office Department, I suggest that what I have said is a clear indication that it is not. I know that condition is true in my own constituency.
However, as regards the hon. member's amendment, and its application to the subject of patronage, I suggest to the leader of the C.C.F. that he study the history of the only government in Canada that really practises patronage, and that is the C.C.F. government is Saskatchewan. The hon. member for Rose-t.own-Biggar will recall that when I was a member of the government of Saskatchewan we retained his services to act as head of a commission to bring in a report on the matter of patronage. He discussed patronage at the time-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member may refer to patronage only as it applies to the Post Office Department.

Then if I am to
limit it to the Post Office Department, I cannot go very far. However, I will say this, that it might be very helpful to pass the bill as the minister has introduced it, and thus give a chance to those C.C.F. chaps in Saskatchewan who now have $5,000-jobs to live up to the platform of the C.C F. party, so that they may resign their jobs and apply for $1,000-jobs with the minister.
There are plenty of them, including defeated candidates and others, who have taken jobs in Saskatchewan, and-
Mr. Chairman, which section are we discussing?

I did not think the leader of the Conservative party would object to a discussion of patronage because that party practised it in the past. I shall not go into the details of what has happened in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member may refer to patronage in connection with the Post Office Department, but not otherwise.

In so far as the
Post Office Department is concerned, the only suggestion I have to make is the one I made a minute ago. By passing this section we will simply permit the appointment to $1,000 jobs of persons who are now making $5,000 in Saskatchewan, many of whom were candidates for this house. The Postmaster General might consider that they had lived up to their platform. If they believe in it then they will cheerfully resign their present $5,000 jobs which were given to them at the expense of the taxpayers of Saskatchewan and will apply to the Postmaster General for these $1,000 jobs. At a later time I shall go into all the details of these 2,000 odd appointments in Saskatchewan.

I do not propose to enter into an argument with the hon. member for Yorkton whom I have known for a long time, but I want to say that as far as I am concerned I have always been opposed to political patronage. I am opposed to it now. If the hon. gentleman wishes to discuss Saskatchewan affairs, the place to do it is in Saskatchewan where I have no doubt he will be answered most adequately by those who have the responsibility of administering affairs in that province.
Will the hon. gentleman say that patronage is not being practised by the government of Saskatchewan?
I am not responsible for what is being done in Saskatchewan, nor is this the place to discuss it.

I do not think this is the time and place to provide a cushion to sit on when we are defeated, which is' something that will happen to a great number of hon. members in the near future. If the hon. member does not know anything more about the Post Office Department than he does about patronage, then he will not be employed. This is a most serious item and it should not be tangled up with patronage; it should be tangled up with the proper method of running the government. This particular item might lead to serious results. How much does it cost the government which is endeavouring in a small way to save public money to call for a tender for a rural mail route? It would cost next to nothing if they did it in a common sense, businesslike manner.
Yet we find the government saying that they are going to leave this to the discretion of a man who is given the right to handle this amount of $1,000 of the taxpayers' money. He is to have the say about the competency of the man who is given the job. He is supposed to pick the best man to do the job. I remember a few years ago when I brought a certain matter to the attention of the department which took the proper action. A man who could not read correctly had been appointed as a rural mail carrier in my constituency. He would take a letter addressed to Mr. Smith and deliver it to Mr. Jones one mile away. I must say that when I brought this matter to the attention of the department they made a thorough investigation and found that my contention was correct, that the man was absolutely incompetent to carry the mail in that district.
He may not have been a good Liberal.

I do not know whether he was a good Liberal or a good Conservative, he was certainly a poor mail carrier. I must say that the government officials recognized that fact and the man was relieved of his duties and a competent person appointed in his place. This is the thin edge of the wedge. It may be only $1,000, but I do not think this principle should be extended at all as it will legd to bad practices.
The human element will enter into appointments of this kind. This is so in municipal, provincial or federal government affairs. I think the minister and his officials have the best motives in the world for requesting this change, but I appeal to them not to take this matter out of the hands of competent Ottawa
Post Office Act
officials or civil servants and place it in the hands, not only of defeated Liberal candidates but I can think of defeated Conservative candidates whom I would not like to trust with so much power.
While I am here it is my duty, as it is the duty of every hon. member, to see that no temptation is placed in the wrong hands especially when it may involve the taxpayers' money. There is a possibility that inefficiency will creep in and will remain unnoticed for months and the people will suffer. That is exactly what happened in the case I brought to the attention of the department. People complained to the postmaster and they went to other people. One or two inspectors came up and looked over the situation, but it required action by a man who meant business. The department wrote to me and said that my contention was quite right and they admitted that this man was delivering one mail one-quarter mile, one-half mile or one mile beyond where it should be delivered.
I can see where this might be permitted in the case of small routes involving $500 or $600, and I would not care whether a Liberal or a Conservative got it. But I know the investigation would not be thorough enough. While I have the utmost respect for the small country postmaster, I do not think the responsibility of making such appointments should be placed on his shoulders. I can understand that in the case of $250 or $300 time might be saved by making a temporary appointment, but when you are going to appoint a permanent rural carrier I do not think this practice should be followed. I remember the old teaching of my father-save the pennies and the dollars will take care of themselves. That is what I am urging now. I do not want to hold up the bill, but if we do not hold it up on these items the consequences may be considerable.
Amendment (Mr. Coldwell) negatived.

On section 23-Postmaster General may contract where amount $1,000 or less.

I have an
amendment to move to this section. I was discussing the old section 73, from which this section is derived, and I had drawn the attention of the Postmaster General to the following phrase in that section:
-when he conceives the public interest will be promoted by such a course;
I see no reason why those words which place a responsibility upon the Postmaster

General should be omitted from the present section, so I should like to move:
That section 23 (1) be amended by inserting at the commencement of the subsection the following words:
"When the Postmaster General conceives the public interest will be promoted by such a course he"

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 24-Lowest tenderer to be accepted except for cause.

This is the section which provides that the lowest tender shall be accepted, except for cause. Generally in commercial contracts the last clause provides something like this: "The lowest or any tender shall not necessarily be accepted." I realize that in dealing with tenders it is good practice usually to accept the lowest, but in some cases there are tenders obviously too low, which in the judgment of the residents of the area cannot be successfully fulfilled. I wonder if the minister would consider some practice such as taking the mean of all tenders submitted on a mileage basis and eliminating those say 20 per cent above the mean or 20 per cent below. I know of one case in particular, the man who was servicing my own district, where the tender was so low the contract could not possibly be fulfilled; as a matter of fact later on the route had to be split into three. But because he was a reputable man the tender was accepted. The facts of the case were not sufficiently investigated, and there was considerable trouble on that route.
There is just one other point in regard to these routes. When that man took over the route there were some 600 people living on it. By the end of the first year that number had increased to something like 1,400, and the number of boxes had almost trebled. I would like the minister to give the formula under which the pay is increased as the number of boxes goes up. My first question is whether there is any method by which a tender which is obviously well below the mean is not accepted, and my second question is what is the formula for extra payments for an increased number of boxes.
The answer to the first question is no. The answer to the second question is none.
You mean if there are 300 boxes and that number increases to 600 the courier gets no more?
Not if there is no increase in mileage. If there is an increase in mileage there is an increase in proportion to the rate of the contract.
I think that is most unfair.
When tenders are called and received, Why does the department write to those tendering and ask them to lower their tenders? Do they write the same letter to all those tendering?
I refer the 'hon. member to section 26 on that point.

Section agreed to.
Section 25 agreed to.
On section 26-Where tenders excessive.

Well, I will ask my question again. Why is it that when tenders are called the department then writes to the men who have tendered, or some of them, telling them their tenders are too high and asking them to reduce them? I thought when tenders were called the department would accept one. I have in mind a case over which we had a lot of trouble, and I am going to name the route so the Postmaster General will know what I am talking about. This was the contract for Vernon Bridge rural route No. 2, which was held by a man named Sullivan for a number of years at the price of $960. His contract expired in 1950. Before it expired the department wrote to him saying the price he was getting was considered too high. Then the department asked him to tender again, though they knew that other contracts for the same mileage were being signed for as much as $1,150. Notwithstanding that they wrote telling him he was too high and wanting him to reduce his price. He did not reduce it, so once more they called for tenders. This time he was the only tenderer at $960, and they had no alternative but to accept that tender, which they did. They sent Sullivan a contract for four years at $960, and Sullivan signed it.
In the meantime a fly got in the ointment. The department wrote that there had been a mistake, that the contract was only for one year, and they sent Sullivan a new contract for one year at $960. This he refused to sign, because he had already signed a contract for four years at the same price. Then the funny

pare of this thing took place. They called for new tenders again, and so it would not seem that they were calling for the same route again the department added an extra mile to it, dressed it up in a new costume and called for tenders. Naturally Sullivan tendered again, and someone else came into the picture with a tender some 30 cents a day lower than Sullivan's. The tenders were opened on December 29, 1950, and the contract was let on January 16, 1951; pretty quick work. That contract was with another man for four years, and for'$l,020. They did not give this faithful courier a ghost of a chance, though on two or three different occasions he had obliged the department by carrying the mail during the war years when they could not get anyone else to do it.
I'll bet he's voting Conservative now.

If he is not, I miss my guess. Deals of this kind are going on all the time; and I am speaking now of my own constituency, which I know. I object to the department writing to a man.who had the contract before and telling him his tender was too high last year, he will have to go lower, and as soon as he consents, then the department sends somebody out to see if they can get another tender at a lower rate. Now, that is not what we should expect from the department. One sees the tendency in every part of this new bill to give more absolute power, to the Postmaster General. After a while it will become so bad it will be difficult to get people to carry the mail at any price. I think that is a question that should be looked into. For instance in my constituency, apart from the side districts, out of the seventy-nine rural contracts that are left fifty-two of them are below $1,000. They should all be let by tender, and more than three weeks should be allowed for advertising

Sections 29 to 32 inclusive agreed to.
On section 33-Increase or alteration of service.

Would the Postmaster General not have authority under this clause to increase the amount paid to a contractor if there had been a substantial increase in the number of boxes along his route? Quite obviously, boxes which are scattered all along a route mean additional expense to the carrier. I would have hoped that something could have been done to influence the patrons to collect their boxes together at a suitable place. As one drives along a country road one can see boxes scattered every fifty yards. As the number of these boxes increases, so does the expense of the courier increase because he has to stop every few yards. Would this clause not give the Postmaster General an opportunity of increasing the amount of a contract where there had been a substantial number of boxes added, although there might not have been any increase in the mileage?

This is the old section 79, and it has always been interpreted as being based on a change in frequency and distance. The reason for interpreting it like that is contained in the lines following the one to which the hon. member was referring which reads:
Where there is a substantial increase or alteration in the service required under a mail contract necessitating additional expenditure by the contractor...
I do not think it adds any additional expense for a contractor to have one or two more boxes. The fact that the frequency is increased or the distance is increased does mean increased expenditure. I do not think an extra box means extra expenditure.

I cannot accept that, because every time you stop a car and start it up again it takes more gasoline and it takes more time. If a certain interpretation has been given to that clause in the old act, surely now that we are having a new act we could have a new and more generous interpretation. The rural courier has a pretty tough time. The increase in the number of boxes in some areas is so great that many of these rural couriers are serving what amount to suburban areas. It is a question of stopping two or three times within a block. Every time the car stops and has to be started up again, it takes more of that man's time and takes more gasoline.

I appreciate the position taken by the hon. member for Nanaimo in trying

Post Office Act
to give me more power than I have been requesting. It makes a difference with some other members.
I do not mind powers if they are used reasonably and intelligently.
Considering the possibility there is to use the additional powers that have been given to me-
I believe those powers are written right into that clause.

That is exactly the point I tried to raise. Years ago in my own constituency there used to be two or three boxes where now there are as many as thirty boxes. Our rural mail man has to stay there for as much as a quarter of an hour to deliver the mail to all those boxes. Sometimes the mail is substantial, and all the time he has to keep his car running. Surely his time must be worth something. The car has to have extra capacity in order to carry the great volume of mail he has to put in the back of it. It is a much more expensive business than it was in the old days. I recall that the rural courier used to be through his job by midday or by one o'clock in the afternoon. Today he has so many boxes to look after he is not through before five or six o'clock. Surely if he were paid a certain amount to do half a day's work, even though the mileage is the same, there must be some formula by which he can be paid more if it takes him a whole day to do the job.
Many rural mail couriers used to have a half day's work to do, but now it is a fulltime job. They used to be able to do other work, but that is precluded. I feel sure there should be some formula in this a?t by which the rural mail courier could be paid on a per box basis over a certain period.
Mr. Chairman, the section has never been interpreted in that way, but after listening to the arguments of the hon. member, perhaps it should be interpreted that way.

May I suggest one other
reason for giving it a more generous interpretation. A few years ago we had a bonus system-
That is what I just said.

No, you did not say that. I am pointing out another reason why you could give it a more generous interpretation. A few years ago there was a bonus system for these rural mail couriers. Now that has been eliminated, and I believe this section gives an opportunity for a more generous interpretation than the old section.

Section agreed to.
Sections 34 to 44 inclusive agreed to.
On section 45-Transportation of United States mail.
Will the minister state how this section will apply to mails going to United States bases in Newfoundland?

I do not know whether this will cover the point that my hon. friend had in mind. This is a reciprocal arrangement and it is covered by the convention between Canada and the United States which reads as follows:
The United States of America and the Dominion of Canada each grants to the other free of any charges, detention or examination whatsoever, the transit across its territory, by all trains that it uses for its own mails, of the closed mails made up by any authorized exchange office of either country addressed to any other exchange office of the same country, or to any exchange office of the other country.
When did this convention come into force?
I have not the date here. I will try to get it.
The point I am making is this. This is a brand new act which is being put in and it is going to be superseded by what has gone on before. I think you would have to amend that particular section.

This section 45 covers the regular international convention or agreement. Maybe what the hon. member has in mind is paragraph (s) to which I drew the attention of hon. members when we were considering section 6. That might be the question the hon. member would like to know about. That paragraph (s) flows from the declaration that was made the other day by the Prime Minister about the Newfoundland bases.
Should it not go farther than the section shows there? What about civilians at those bases? Is that not to apply to them at all?
No. Civilians are covered by the ordinary postal laws.
I mean civilians in the sense of wives of service personnel. Where do they fit in?

I think that section 6 (s) covers the whole point. If there are any particulars the hon. member would like to have, if he will call at my office, we can give him anything that he wishes. All the necessary authority is in the act at the present time.

If the minister is satisfied, all right. I am far from satisfied that that

section is right as it is, but if the minister does not wish to amend it, I do not want it to be amended. I may say quite frankly, however, that I do not think it is right as it is.

Section agreed to.
Sections 46 to 74 inclusive agreed to.
On section 75-Evidence.

I do not want to spoil this perfect holiday so far, Mr. Chairman, but I gather that the term "royal mail" is no longer applicable. The section reads as follows:
In any prosecution under this act evidence that any thing bears the words "Post Office," "Canada Post Office," "Canada Mail" or any similar expression is prima facie proof that the thing was established or authorized for use in connection with the Canada Post Office under the authority of this act.
I understand that the term "royal mail" now has no significance in Canada.
The hon. member will notice that the name of the act is "An act respecting the Canada Post Office."
Yes. But this term "royal mail" is now an obsolete term in Canada. That is the point I am getting at.
Yes.
I regret that.

Just a minute, Mr. Chairman. I want to say a word on section 78.
Post Office Act
I realize that it is unusual to get an amendment through around here, but I just wish to make a brief comment on this section for the repeal of various items of legislation now on the statute books, including part IX of the Excise Tax Act. The repeal of that legislation has to be looked at in conjunction with section 10 which we have already passed. Part IX of the Excise Tax Act which is now being repealed is the part of the Excise Tax Act which imposes taxation on the delivery of letters or post cards by post.
I wish to remind members of the committee that when the taxation in part IX of the Excise Tax Aot was placed before the house, it was clearly stated that it was a tax for war purposes only. Some hon. members whose memories go back quite a few years will recall the days when the Liberals had a good deal to say about the restoration of penny postage, "penny" of course being used in the English sense of two cents. But when the war came there was brought into being the Special War Revenue Act which later became the Excise Tax Act, and in the early years one cent was added to the postage rate which was formerly on the penny postage basis. The first tax of one cent increased the rate for letters from two cents to three cents. Then in 1943, when Mr. Ilsley brought in his budget of that year, he announced a further tax, or in other words an increase in the tax on letters. The result of the tax of 1943 was that the rate on letters became four cents, two cents of which was postage and two cents of which was tax. When questioned about this matter on April 25, 1943, the Postmaster General of that day made it clear that this was a tax for war purposes and not postage. I should like to quote a bit from page 1851 of Hansard of April 5, 1943, which reads as follows:

This means that
the extra cent -
That is, the increase from one cent of tax to two cents of tax, making a total of four cents per letter.
-is an excise tax, not postage?

That is correct. The postage has
not been raised. But my colleague the Minister of Finance has required extra money for the war expenditure. It'was estimated that something upwards of $8 million could be raised by an additional one cent on letters and post cards. It was not that the Post Office Department required more money for operating. In fact our surplus as shown in the report has increased substantially in the last few years, from some $3,250 to upward of $4,500,000, with every indication that it will be still higher, although the final figures for the fiscal year are not yet in.
The point I wish to make is that when the postage on letters was boosted first from two cents to three cents, and then later to

Post Office Act
four cents it was made clear by the Postmaster General and by the minister of finance of that day that that four cents was not all postage; it was two cents postage and two cents tax for purposes of war revenue. Today, without much notice being paid to it, we have had laid before us a proposal which builds that two cents, which has been on during these years as a matter of tax, into the postage rate structure. It may be that increased costs make this change necessary. It may be that the idea of penny postage, in view of what has happened to the value of money, is gone. But I felt that before we passed this last section we should know what we are doing. We are changing the basis of our four cent postage rate from what it has been for years, two cents postage and two cents tax, to four cents postage-
One cent-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The hon. member for Leeds is saying "one cent". No; I thought that myself this afternoon, but I went to the library and looked it up, and found that the postage rate was two cents, and that at first one cent tax was put on. I cannot tell you precisely the year, but it was probably in the early years of the war. Then in 1943 when Mr. Usley brought in his budget of that year he had this as clause 1 in his resolution regarding the Special War Revenue Act:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Special War Revenue Act and to provide:
(1) That the excise tax on each letter transmitted by post be increased from one to two cents.
It was already one cent tax and two cents postage. It became two cents tax and two cents postage. It has been that way from 1943 to the present. What we are now doing is repealing the tax but raising the postage to the figure of four cents.

Section agreed to.
On the title.

Before the title carries I want to ask the Postmaster General one question. I notice that in this bill nothing has been said about philatelists. I understand there is a special philatelic section of the post office. No mention is made of that section in this bill. Is that done purposely, or can the minister explain why? I understand that there is a special Canadian philatelic exhibition this summer which has the blessing of the department. I just want that one point cleared up.

It could certainly be covered by section five, which reads:
Subject to this act, the Postmaster General shall administer, superintend and manage the Canada Post Office-

It could certainly come under that.
It could?
Yes.

It is rather late in the
evening to start discussion, but if there is no objection I have some comments I should like to make. I make no excuse for speaking on this subject, coming as I do from a province that produces one-third of all the fish caught in Canada. The Newfoundland catch is roughly equal to that of the maritime provinces and Quebec, and the remaining one-third is made up of British Columbia and the great lakes fisheries.
iLast year the marketed value of the dominion's fisheries, that is the entire fisheries of the dominion-I suppose I should now say of Canada-amounted to approximately $180 million. Newfoundland's share of this amount was not one-third, but one-sixth. The reason for the difference in the returns for the Newfoundland product and that of the rest of the dominion is that the other provinces catch a greater variety of fish, particularly the more highly priced varieties such as lobster, than does Newfoundland. Whilst Newfoundland caught approximately the same quantity of fish as the maritime provinces and Quebec, those provinces received twice as much in payment for their products.
Better fish.

Not a bit of it; don't let anybody tell you that. Quebec and the mari-times sell greater quantities of their fish fresh; whereas the product of Newfoundland is sold as a dry salted fish, and consequently it can be sold only in the lower priced markets.
It is true that in Newfoundland we are producing more and more fresh frozen fish; but
Supply-Fisheries
for many years, until the market has been converted, Newfoundland will have to depend, in the selling of her fish, to a very large extent on the salt fish trade. And as this fish is sold principally to the countries in the sterling group, the question of the convertibility of sterling is one of the greatest, perhaps the greatest problem, in connection with fisheries in Newfoundland.
That is a problem which, as the minister realizes, will continue for years to come. I trust that those of us from Newfoundland who sit in this and in future parliaments will not have continually to be bringing this problem of convertibility to the attention of the present minister and his successors; because it is a problem which will continue for many years to come, before the fish trade switches to fresh frozen fish. As the minister is aware, and possibly some hon. members are not, the Newfoundland salt codfish trade has continued practically without interruption for some four centuries. Before Newfoundland joined Canada, she received preferential treatment from Great Britain in this particular connection. There is no question in my mind or, I am sure, in the mind of the minister or the minds of those associated with him in the department, that there is no better service Canada could render to its newest province than to see to it that this particular currency problem is looked after regularly.
When the minister made his statement with regard to convertibility, I joined with the hon. member for Trinity-Conception in saying that I welcomed that statement, in which it was pointed out that convertibility was being arranged for this year. While the arrangement has been made only to the extent of $4 million, I feel if it comes to the point where we have to arrange for an extra $2 million, we will not be knocking at a completely closed door.
There is no doubt about the fact that unless we in Newfoundland continue to make our sales of salt codfish to Mediterranean countries, and this sterling problem is satisfactorily handled, it will be a serious matter for our province-and serious not only for Newfoundland, but also for the maritime provinces and Quebec. It means that if we are not able to sell in these age-old markets we have had, and try to sell in markets in which fish from the maritime provinces and Quebec is being sold now, it will seriously interfere with their markets for that type of fish.
It is for that reason therefore I say that the maritime and Quebec members should not feel in any way jealous of what they may consider as Dreferential treatment, in

Supply-Fisheries
so far as the arrangement for the convertibility of sterling, for Newfoundland is concerned. Because without this arrangement for convertibility, and with Newfoundland challenging the markets enjoyed by the mari-times and Quebec, it would be catastrophic for all these provinces. That is why I say there should not be any real difficulty in so far as appreciating the problem is concerned, when the members from those provinces understand that situation.
It is generally admitted that Canada is one of the great exporting countries of the world. It may be of interest to hon. members to point out that the ratio of exports of Newfoundland to its gross national production is practically three times as great as that of the dominion as a whole. Newfoundland's ratio of export trade to total national income is 67 per cent, whereas the ratio of the dominion is approximately 24 per cent. Newfoundland's ratio of imports is about 85 per cent while that of Canada as a whole is 21 per cent. The over-all picture therefore indicates clearly how our export trade works considerably to the benefit of the country as a whole. As I have pointed out, and as has been pointed out by hon. members before, the great bulk of exports from our newest province is to countries dealing in dollars. Those dollars are American dollars, and they aid materially in the economy of Canada as a whole.
But the fishing industry, in so far as salted fish is concerned, because of the particular circumstances I have pointed out, does require preferential treatment, and will continue to need it for many years to come. The chief reason is that by far the largest percentage of the working force of Newfoundland is directly engaged in fisheries, and the money goes directly back to those people.
Then, we come down to the type of fish caught. There are three types, namely Labrador, shore and bank. As the name implies, the Labrador fish are caught in Labrador waters, while the shore fish are caught along the shores of Newfoundland, and the bank fish are caught on the Grand Banks.
In view of the higher cost of living, as it has been going up in the last year, and in view of the low prices which prevailed last year for fish, it appears to me that the fishermen will have to have an increase of at least from 30 to 35 per cent in the prices of their f\ph, if they are to get through successfully at all, even with a good average voyage.
With all due respect to the minister, and the hopes he expressed in his statement on May 17, particularly his belief that the prices are going to be good this year, I doubt very 
much whether they will be as good as he thought they would be. If they are going to be good, they are certainly not going to keep up with the increased cost of living. Consequently fishermen will not be any better off.
And this gets back to the statement made by the retiring president of the fisheries council of Canada at its sixth meeting in Ottawa in March last, when he said:
The fisheries would seem to afford a great opportunity to Canadians to demonstrate the democratic way of life. Fishing is a noble, a wholesome, venturesome calling. It should bring forth the best that is in the fisherman and businessman, but I submit the industry will have failed in its destiny if the fisherman has not prospered and enjoyed a fair measure of the good things of life.
That should be the keynote of the fishing industry; it is the keynote, I am sure, of what the minister is trying to do, the keynote of what those associated with him in the department and in the fisheries council are trying to do-to give the ordinary, common fisherman a better share of the good things of life. I submit the only way the ordinary fisherman, as I know him, is going to be given a fair share of the good things of life is to have his catch sold in such a way that he will have a better return than he is getting at the present time.
This gets right back to what we have been talking about for some time. Newfoundland members have not been squawking unnecessarily; they have just been trying to make their point clear-and I believe the minister is aware of that. I believe I am justified once again in asking him that very, very serious consideration be given to setting a floor price for fish. I know the minister has given this matter consideration and I know he has had the advice of the prices support board. I know also that he is aware of a meeting that took place last week in St. John's between the fishermen and the salt codfish association. I understand that the minister stated the other day that there was not a great difference between the prices asked and what the merchants were prepared to pay. I do not know whether the minister is prepared to indicate what those prices are because if he is not I will be arguing more or less in the dark. The price that has been asked by the fishermen for the best grade fish I understand is around $12 per quintal, and I do not think that has been met. That would not appear to be an unfair price to ask. I am not saying that it is or is not, that is just what I am told.
This is not an altogether new problem. We have had price support for other commodities produced in Canada. Our friends from, the west have seen their commodities subsidized extensively and I

believe there is still a hot argument as to whether proper payment has been made for wheat. We have had subsidies on potatoes and cheese and I see no reason why the same principle should not be applied to fish. In the brief submitted in 1944 by the United Maritime Fisheries, as a result of which the Fisheries Prices Support Act was passed, the following statement appears:
It is the view of our members that, if the fishery is to be reconstructed upon a basis that will provide freedom from want for the fishermen, some means must be devised to maintain fish prices on a parity with other commodities. If the price structure in other branches of food production is to be supported by a floor, it is equally necessary to make a similar provision for the fishery. It is well known that in the past the discrepancy between the prices received by the primary producer and the general commodity levels has been greater in the fishery than in any other branch of production.
The concluding paragraph of that brief reads:
We urge, therefore, that in order to ensure our fishermen a reasonable measure of security, a floor be established under fish prices on a basis which will put them on an equal footing with other producers.
I understand that Norway and Iceland, both of which are competitors of Canada in the sale of salt fish, have established floor prices.	I believe that this information,
which I obtained from a departmental publication, is correct.
I am not too well prepared tonight at this late hour and for a moment I shall leave fish and deal with another part of the fisheries that comes under the minister, our seal fisheries. As the minister is aware, there was considerable competition in sealing this year from the Norwegians and other nationalities. The killing date of March 13 was established many years ago by Newfoundland, which date gave the seals time to deliver their young. This year the Norwegian sealers came in without waiting for that date and the seals were killed before they had a chance to deliver their young. This was very cruel killing and it has been commented upon strongly by the Newfoundland press. In the Daily News of April 2 Captain Sidney Hill of the Arctic Sealer commented on this fact as follows:
A crime was committed, one for which there should be no excuse. I saw the crews of the ships sculping the whitecoats within a few hours after they were born. Many of these seals were not more than twelve pounds in weight. The Norwegian and other ships were taking seals ar.11 this forced all ships to do the same. There should be some international agreement made to prohibit the taking of young harps before the old Newfoundland killing
Supply-Fisheries
date, March 13. It is a murder to take the seals so early and I cannot condemn the practice too strongly.
In the Evening Telegram of April 19 appeared a strong editorial headed, "The .sealing industry imperilled." I shall not read it all, but there is one paragraph dealing with this type of slaughter which reads:
That is a matter of importance. The other damning aspect of this early killing is that the slaughter is perpetrated so soon after, or even before, propagation occurs, to the complete disregard of all the laws of conservation. It is asking men to engage in a barbarous slaughter. It is also asking them to disregard laws which have been made to ensure that species, no matter what kind, will not become extinct. Under such unregulated conditions it is futile to expect that the seals can long survive.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
